body.text: Upāyahṛdayam /
body.translated_text: <s>Upāyahṛdayam</s> (The Heart of Method)

body.text: atha prathamaṃ prakaraṇam /
body.translated_text: Now, the first chapter.

children.translated_text: Through the understanding of this debate, understanding of the principles of debate [is achieved];
And this profound subject is here explained in detail.

body.text: vādo na kartavyaḥ / kasmāt? prāyeṇa hi vādakārakāṇāṃ sañjātavipulakrodhamadamattānāṃ svayaṃ vibhrāntacittānāṃ manaso 'natimṛdutā parapāpaprakāśakatvaṃ svapāṇḍityānumodakatvañcetyādayo doṣā budhirnirbhatsitāḥ / tasmādāryajanā asaṃkhyeyopāyairvivādachedakāstatparihāraprītāśca viṣabhājanaparityāgādiva / vādakārakāṇāñcāntaraṃ vastuto mṛdvapi paraṃ bahirbahudoṣaṃ dṛśyate / tasmātsvahitaparahitābhilāṣiṇaite vivādadharmāḥ praheyāḥ /
body.translated_text: Debate should not be undertaken. Why? Because generally, for those who engage in debate, intoxicated with the arising of great anger and pride, their own minds confused — harshness of mind, the tendency to expose others' faults, and self-congratulation on one's own learning — these and other faults are condemned by the wise. Therefore, noble people cut off disputes through countless means and delight in avoiding them, just as one avoids a vessel of poison. And among debaters, though their disposition may in reality be mild within, outwardly many faults are seen. Therefore, for those who desire their own and others' welfare, these habits of disputation should be abandoned.

body.text: atrocyate / maivaṃ, naiṣa vādaprārambhaḥ paribhavalābhakhyātyartho 'pi tu sulakṣaṇadurlakṣaṇopadeśecchayaiva vādasya prārambhaḥ /
body.translated_text: To this it is said: Not so! This undertaking of debate is not for the purpose of humiliation, profit, or fame; rather, the undertaking of debate is solely for the purpose of teaching good characteristics and bad characteristics.

body.text: yadīha loke vādo na bhavet, mugdhānāṃ bāhulyaṃ syāt / tataśca laukikamithyājñānakuśalatāsahacarabhrāntisamudbhūtakukarmabhiḥ saṃsāradurgatiḥ sadarthahāniśca /
body.translated_text: If there were no debate in this world, the number of deluded people would increase. And then, through evil deeds arising from worldly delusion accompanied by skill in false knowledge, there would be miserable rebirths in <s>saṃsāra</s> and loss of true purpose.

body.text: vādāvagame tu svayaṃ sulakṣadurlakṣaṇaśūnyalakṣaṇaparijñānatvāt sarve mārāstīrthikā mithyādṛṣṭimanuṣyāśca viheṭhanāsamarthā (#Uh 4#) apratibandhakārāśca / tasmātsattvahitecchayeha loke saddharmasya pracārecchayā ca mayaiṣa samyagvāda ārabhyate /
body.translated_text: When debate is understood, however, through one's own complete knowledge of good characteristics, bad characteristics, and empty characteristics, all <s>Māras</s>, <s>tīrthikas</s> (heterodox teachers), and people of wrong views are unable to cause harm and unable to create obstacles. Therefore, with the desire for the welfare of beings and with the wish to spread the true <s>Dharma</s> in this world, this correct debate is undertaken by me.

body.text: yathāsraphalaparipuṣṭikāmena tat(phala)parirakṣaṇārthaṃ bahirbahutīkṣṇakaṇṭakanikaravinyāsaḥ kriyate /
body.translated_text: Just as one who desires the full ripening of fruit arranges numerous sharp thorns outside for the purpose of protecting that fruit,

body.text: vādārambho 'pi tathaivādhunā saddharmmarakṣaṇecchayā na tu khyātilābhāya / yaduktaṃ (bhavatā) pūrvaṃ [eṣa vādo] vivādapravardhaka iti / tadayuktam / dharmarakṣaṇārthameva hi vāda ārabdhavyaḥ /
body.translated_text: so too the undertaking of debate now is for the wish to protect the true <s>Dharma</s>, not for fame or profit. What you previously said — that 'this debate promotes dispute' — is unjustified. For debate should be undertaken solely for the protection of <s>Dharma</s>.

body.text: āha / yaduktaṃ pūrvaṃ bhavatā yadyetaṃ vādaṃ jānīyādvādadharmānavagacchediti vaktavyametasya lakṣaṇam /
body.translated_text: [The opponent] says: What you previously said — that if one knows this debate, one understands the principles of debate — the characteristics of this should be stated.

body.text: atrocyate / tasya vādasyāṣṭavidho bhedaḥ / tadarthagatiprajñānasāmarthye paravādāvagamaḥ, yathā dhānyamuptvā siktā codakena tasya puṣṭiḥ samṛddhiśca sādhyate / tṛṇādyanutsāraṇe tūṭkṛṣṭāṅkurā na jāyante / yadi kaścidetamaṣṭāvidhaṃ [vādaṃ] śṛṇuyādarthantu tasya nāvagacchettadā [tasya] sarveṣu vādeṣu saṃśayo bhavet / yadi kaścidetamaṣṭavidhamarthaṃ parijānīyānniyatameva sarvavādadharmāvagame samartho bhavet /
body.translated_text: To this it is said: That debate has eight divisions. When one has the capacity for wisdom in understanding their meaning, one comprehends the opponent's arguments — just as when grain is sown and irrigated with water, its growth and prosperity are achieved. But when weeds are not removed, excellent sprouts do not grow. If someone hears this eightfold [debate] but does not understand its meaning, then there would be doubt in all debates. If someone fully knows this eightfold meaning, he would certainly be capable of understanding all principles of debate.

body.text: āha / etadvādaparijñānādeva vādadharmā niyatamavagamyanta iti (bhavato)ktam / atha tīrthikānāṃ vādadharmāḥ santi na vā / atrocyate santyeva / yathā vaiśeṣikāṇāṃ ṣaṭ padārthāḥ / dravyaṃ guṇaḥ sāmānyaṃ viśeṣaḥ karma samavāyaścetyādikavādadharmeṣu svavagateṣvapi parasūtraśāstrāṇāmapratītiḥ /
body.translated_text: [The opponent] says: It was said by you that from the complete knowledge of this debate, the principles of debate are certainly understood. Now, do the <s>tīrthikas</s> have principles of debate or not? To this it is said: They certainly exist. For example, the <s>Vaiśeṣikas</s> have six categories (<s>padārthas</s>): substance (<s>dravya</s>), quality (<s>guṇa</s>), universal (<s>sāmānya</s>), particularity (<s>viśeṣa</s>), action (<s>karma</s>), and inherence (<s>samavāya</s>). Even though they understand such principles of their own debate, they do not comprehend the <s>sūtras</s> and treatises of others.

body.text: ato vādanayapratipādanārthaṃ prapañcocchedanārthañcaite 'ṣṭavidhā gambhīrāḥ sadvādadharmāḥ saṃkṣepato mayā kathyante / (#Uh 5#) dṛṣṭāntaḥ siddhānto vākyapraśaṃsā vākyadoṣaḥ pramāṇaṃ prāptakālavākyaṃ hetvābhāso vākchalam /
body.translated_text: Therefore, for the purpose of establishing the method of debate and for the purpose of cutting off conceptual proliferation (<s>prapañca</s>), these eight profound principles of correct debate are briefly stated by me: <s>dṛṣṭānta</s> (illustration), <s>siddhānta</s> (established conclusion), <s>vākyapraśaṃsā</s> (praise of statement), <s>vākyadoṣa</s> (fault of statement), <s>pramāṇa</s> (means of valid knowledge), <s>prāptakālavākya</s> (timely statement), <s>hetvābhāsa</s> (fallacious reasoning), and <s>vākchala</s> (verbal quibbling).

body.text: dṛṣṭānto dvividhaḥ / saṃpūrṇadṛṣṭānta āśiṃkadṛṣṭāntaśca / siddhānto niścitārtha iti / vākyapraśaṃsā vākyasyārthānugamaḥ / vākyadoṣo vākyasya yuktivyatyayaḥ / pramāṇaṃ dvividhajñāpakaheturutpattiheturvyañjanahetuśca / prāptakāla vākyam / yathā yadi pūrvaṃ dhātvāyatanāni vadet / paścāttu pañcaskandhān tadaitadaprāptakālamityucyate / prāptakālavākyaṃ tu vākyakramāvagame / hetvābhāso yathā marīcābudakābhāsaḥ, na tu vastuta udakam / yadi vādī svalaṅkṛtairvākyairudakamiti vadettadā sa hetvābhāsaḥ / vākchalaṃ yathā / navakambala ityukte taddūṣayan vadet / vastraṃ na kālaḥ kathaṃ nava ityucyate / iti chalam / evaṃ samāmato 'ṣṭavidho 'rthaḥ samākhyātaḥ / idānīṃ krameṇa tallakṣaṇāni vistareṇa vyākhyāsyāmaḥ /
body.translated_text: <s>Dṛṣṭānta</s> (illustration) is twofold: complete illustration (<s>saṃpūrṇadṛṣṭānta</s>) and partial illustration (<s>āśiṃkadṛṣṭānta</s>). <s>Siddhānta</s> (established conclusion) is a determined meaning. <s>Vākyapraśaṃsā</s> (praise of statement) is comprehension of the meaning of a statement. <s>Vākyadoṣa</s> (fault of statement) is the reversal of the reasoning in a statement. <s>Pramāṇa</s> (means of valid knowledge) is of two kinds: the cause that makes known, the cause of arising, and the cause of indication. <s>Prāptakālavākya</s> (timely statement): for example, if one first speaks of the elements (<s>dhātus</s>) and sense-bases (<s>āyatanas</s>), but afterward of the five aggregates (<s>skandhas</s>), then that is called untimely. But a timely statement [accords with] the understanding of the proper sequence of statements. <s>Hetvābhāsa</s> (fallacious reasoning) is like the appearance of water in a mirage — but it is not in reality water. If a debater with well-adorned statements says 'it is water,' then that is a fallacious reason. <s>Vākchala</s> (verbal quibbling) is as follows: when '<s>navakambala</s>' (new blanket) is said, the one refuting it says: 'A cloth is not time — how can it be called "nine" (<s>nava</s>)?' — this is quibbling. Thus the eightfold meaning has been briefly explained. Now we shall explain those characteristics in detail in sequence.

body.text: āha / ukto bhavatā pūrvaṃ dṛṣṭāntaḥ / kastāvadupāyo dṛṣṭāntasya sthāpane / atrocyate / dṛṣṭāntavacanaṃ hi yatra pṛthagjanānāmāryāṇāñca buddhisāmyaṃ tadā vaktavyam / yathā cittaṃ cañcalaṃ drutavāyuvat / sarveṣāṃ janānāṃ vāyucāñcalyasya pratīteḥ / tadā cittasthiratāyā niścayaḥ / apratītau dṛṣṭāntālābhaḥ / āha / kasmātsadartha eva nocyate 'pi tu dṛṣṭāntaḥ / atrocyate / dṛṣṭāntavacanaṃ hi sadarthadyotanārtham /
body.translated_text: [The opponent] says: Illustration was mentioned by you before. What then is the method for establishing an illustration? To this it is said: An illustration should be stated where there is equality of understanding between ordinary people (<s>pṛthagjanas</s>) and noble ones (<s>āryas</s>). For example: 'The mind is restless, like a swift wind.' Because all people have experience of the restlessness of wind, there is then certainty about the [lack of] stability of the mind. When there is no [shared] experience, an illustration cannot be obtained. [The opponent] says: Why is the actual meaning itself not stated, but rather an illustration? To this it is said: An illustration is for the purpose of illuminating the actual meaning.

body.text: āha / bhavatā pūrvamuktam pṛthagjanānāmāryāṇāñca buddhisāmyadṛṣṭāntalābha iti / kiṃ sāmyaṃ ko vā viśeṣaḥ / atrocyate / pūrvavat / vāyudṛṣṭāntasya sāmyamityucyate / (#Uh 6#) āryāṇāṃ nirvāṇaprāptiḥ pṛthagjanānāṃ tvaprāptirayaṃ viśeṣa ityucyate /
body.translated_text: [The opponent] says: You previously said that an illustration is obtained where there is equality of understanding between ordinary people and noble ones. What is the equality, and what is the difference? To this it is said: As before — the equality of the wind-illustration is stated. The attainment of <s>nirvāṇa</s> by noble ones, but the non-attainment by ordinary people — this is called the difference.

body.text: āha / uktaṃ dṛṣṭāntalakṣaṇam / kiṃ punaḥ siddhāntalakṣaṇam / atrocyate / sādhyasya hetubhirvistareṇa sthāpanaṃ nirṇayaśca / etatsiddhāntalakṣaṇam /
body.translated_text: [The opponent] says: The characteristics of illustration have been stated. What then are the characteristics of an established conclusion (<s>siddhānta</s>)? To this it is said: The extensive establishment and determination of what is to be proved through reasons — this is the characteristic of an established conclusion.

body.text: āha / siddhāntadharmāḥ kiyantaḥ / atrocyate / catvāraḥ / sarvasamaḥ sarvabhinna ādau samaḥ paścādbhinna ādau bhinnaḥ paścātsamaśca / āha / adhunā bhavataitāni catvāri lakṣaṇāni vyākhyātavyāni /
body.translated_text: [The opponent] says: How many types of established conclusions are there? To this it is said: Four — entirely the same (<s>sarvasama</s>), entirely different (<s>sarvabhinna</s>), initially the same but later different, and initially different but later the same. [The opponent] says: Now these four characteristics should be explained by you.

body.text: atrocyate / arthasthāpanamicchatā caturvidhaṃ jñānamāśrayitavyam / kiṃ taccaturvidham / pratyakṣamanumānamupamānamāgamaśca /
body.translated_text: To this it is said: One who wishes to establish a position must rely on fourfold knowledge. What is that fourfold [knowledge]? <s>Pratyakṣa</s> (direct perception), <s>anumāna</s> (inference), <s>upamāna</s> (comparison), and <s>āgama</s> (scriptural testimony).

body.text: sarvasamo yathā, (vādī vadeda)ātmātmīyañca na vidyete, prativadyapi vadedātmātmīyañca na vidyeta ityayaṃ sarvasamaḥ / sarvabhinno yathā, (vādī vadet) pṛthagiti prativādī tu vadedekamityayam sarvabhinnaḥ / ādau samaḥ paścādbhinno yathā, (vādī vadet) sarvaṃ dṛṣṭadharmaṃ sat / ātmā punarapratyakṣo 'pi sag / prativādī vadedyatpratyakṣadharmakaṃ tadeva saditi vaktavyam / ātmā cedapratyakṣaḥ kathaṃ san / anumānena cedātmā sanniti tarhi pratyakṣapūrvakamanumānamiti / apratyakṣadharmaka ātmā kathamanumīyate / yadi punarupamānenātmā sanniti, atha sādharmyapūrvakamupamānamityātmā kenopamīyate / yadi tvāgamenātmā siddha ityucyate tadayuktam / durbodhaṃ hi sūtram / kutracitsanniti kutracidasanniti kathaṃ tatpratītirityayamādau samaḥ paścādbhinnaḥ / ādau bhinnaḥ (#Uh 7#) paścātsamo yathā, (vādī vadeda)ātmātmīyañca na vidyete / prativādī tu vadedastyātmā, asti puruṣaḥ / nirvāṇābhyupagamastrūbhayorvādinoḥ / ayamucyata bhinnaḥ paścātsamaḥ /
body.translated_text: 'Entirely the same' is, for example: the proponent says 'the self and what belongs to the self do not exist,' and the opponent also says 'the self and what belongs to the self do not exist' — this is 'entirely the same.' 'Entirely different' is, for example: the proponent says 'multiple' and the opponent says 'one' — this is 'entirely different.' 'Initially the same, later different' is, for example: the proponent says 'everything perceived is real; moreover, the self, though imperceptible, is also real.' The opponent says: 'Only what has the nature of being perceptible should be said to be real. If the self is imperceptible, how can it be real? If the self is real through inference, then inference requires prior perception — how can the self, which is imperceptible, be inferred? If the self is real through comparison, then comparison requires prior similarity — with what is the self compared? If the self is said to be established through scripture, that is unjustified, for the <s>sūtra</s> is hard to understand: somewhere it says "exists," somewhere "does not exist" — how is there certainty about that?' — this is 'initially the same, later different.' 'Initially different, later the same' is, for example: the proponent says 'the self and what belongs to the self do not exist'; the opponent says 'the self exists, the person (<s>puruṣa</s>) exists.' But both debaters accept <s>nirvāṇa</s>. This is called 'initially different, later the same.'

body.text: api cāparimitāni lakṣaṇāni siddhāntasya, tadyathā dvādaśa nidānāni, duḥkhaṃ, samudayaḥ, nirodhaḥ, mārgaḥ saptatriṃśatpakṣāḥ, catvāri śrāmaṇyaphalānītyādayo dharmā buddhasya samyagarthā ityucyante /
body.translated_text: Moreover, the characteristics of established conclusions are limitless, such as the twelve links of dependent origination (<s>dvādaśa nidānas</s>), suffering (<s>duḥkha</s>), origination (<s>samudaya</s>), cessation (<s>nirodha</s>), and the path (<s>mārga</s>), the thirty-seven wings of awakening, the four fruits of the ascetic life (<s>śrāmaṇyaphala</s>) — these and other <s>dharmas</s> are said to be the correct teachings of the <s>Buddha</s>.

body.text: sandhyāpūjā, balidānaṃ, dhūpadīpanaṃ, tailadīpanivedanamiti caturvidhā yājñikatīrthikānāṃ kriyā /
body.translated_text: Twilight worship (<s>sandhyāpūjā</s>), offering of food-oblations (<s>balidāna</s>), incense-lighting (<s>dhūpadīpana</s>), and offering of oil-lamps (<s>tailadīpanivedana</s>) — these are the fourfold rituals of the sacrificial <s>tīrthikas</s>.

body.text: triṣaṣṭyakṣarāṇāṃ caturṇāṃ ca padānāmartha iti śābdikāstīrthikāḥ /
body.translated_text: The meaning of sixty-three letters and four words — thus [teach] the grammarian <s>tīrthikas</s>.

body.text: oṣadhividyā ṣaḍvidhā / oṣadhināma, oṣadhiguṇaḥ, oṣadhirasaḥ, oṣadhivīryaṃ, sannipātaḥ, vipākaśceti bhaiṣājyadharmāḥ /
body.translated_text: The science of herbs (<s>oṣadhividyā</s>) is sixfold: name of the herb, quality of the herb, taste of the herb, potency of the herb, combination (<s>sannipāta</s>), and post-digestive transformation (<s>vipāka</s>) — these are the principles of medicine.

body.text: ṣaṭpadārthā vaiśeṣikāṇām //
body.translated_text: The six categories (<s>padārthas</s>) of the <s>Vaiśeṣikas</s>.

body.text: pradhanasyaikyaṃ puruṣā bahavaḥ / [teṣāṃ ca] vimuktiriti sāṃkhyāḥ /
body.translated_text: The oneness of <s>pradhāna</s> (primordial matter) and the multiplicity of <s>puruṣas</s> (souls), and their liberation — thus [teach] the <s>Sāṃkhyas</s>.

body.text: aṣṭau sūkṣmāṇi yathā / catvāri mahābhūtāni buddhirākāśo, vidyā, avidyā, aṣṭaiśvaryāṇi [tadyathā] aṇimā, mahimā, laghimā, prāptiḥ, prākāmyaṃ, kāyavibhāgaḥ, īśitvaṃ tirobhāvaśca / iti yogatīrthikāḥ /
body.translated_text: The eight subtle [entities] are as follows: the four great elements (<s>mahābhūtas</s>), intellect (<s>buddhi</s>), space (<s>ākāśa</s>), knowledge (<s>vidyā</s>), and ignorance (<s>avidyā</s>). The eight supernatural powers (<s>aiśvaryas</s>) are: <s>aṇimā</s> (minuteness), <s>mahimā</s> (greatness), <s>laghimā</s> (lightness), <s>prāpti</s> (attainment), <s>prākāmya</s> (irresistible will), <s>kāyavibhāga</s> (bodily division), <s>īśitva</s> (sovereignty), and <s>tirobhāva</s> (invisibility) — thus [teach] the Yoga <s>tīrthikas</s>.

body.text: jīvo 'jīvaḥ pāpaṃ puṇyamāśravaḥ, nirjarā, sambaraḥ, bandhaḥ, mokṣaḥ / pañcajñānāni [tadyathā] śrutajñānaṃ, matijñānaṃ, avadhijñānaṃ, manaḥparyāyajñānaṃ, kevalajñānam / ṣaḍāvaraṇāni, (#Uh 8#) darśanāvaraṇaṃ, duḥkhavedanīyāvaraṇaṃ, mohāvaraṇamāyurāvaraṇaṃ, gotrāvaraṇaṃ, nāmāvaraṇañca / catvāraḥ kaṣāyāḥ [tadyathā] krodhaḥ, mānaḥ, lābhaḥ, māyā ceti nirgranthadharmāḥ /
body.translated_text: <s>Jīva</s> (soul), <s>ajīva</s> (non-soul), <s>pāpa</s> (sin), <s>puṇya</s> (merit), <s>āśrava</s> (influx), <s>nirjarā</s> (dissipation), <s>saṁvara</s> (stoppage), <s>bandha</s> (bondage), <s>mokṣa</s> (liberation). Five knowledges, namely: <s>śrutajñāna</s> (scriptural knowledge), <s>matijñāna</s> (sensory knowledge), <s>avadhijñāna</s> (clairvoyant knowledge), <s>manaḥparyāyajñāna</s> (telepathic knowledge), and <s>kevalajñāna</s> (omniscient knowledge). Six obscurations (<s>āvaraṇas</s>): (Uh 8) obscuration of perception (<s>darśanāvaraṇa</s>), obscuration of painful feeling (<s>duḥkhavedanīyāvaraṇa</s>), obscuration of delusion (<s>mohāvaraṇa</s>), obscuration of lifespan (<s>āyurāvaraṇa</s>), obscuration of lineage (<s>gotrāvaraṇa</s>), and obscuration of name (<s>nāmāvaraṇa</s>). Four passions (<s>kaṣāyas</s>), namely: anger (<s>krodha</s>), pride (<s>māna</s>), greed (<s>lābha</s>), and deceit (<s>māyā</s>) — these are the doctrines of the <s>Nirgranthas</s> (Jains).

body.text: apare 'pi santi ye vadanti sarvamekaṃ sadbhāvājjñeyam / sarvadharmāṇāṃ ca guṇavattvādaikyam, kiñca pradhānāt samutpannaṃ sarvamekaṃ jñeyamekamūlatvā ityevamekavādinastīrthikāḥ /
body.translated_text: There are also others who say: everything is one, to be known through its quality of existence. And because all <s>dharmas</s> possess qualities, there is oneness. Moreover, everything arises from <s>Pradhāna</s> (primal matter), [therefore] everything is one, to be known as having a single root — thus [speak] the <s>Ekavādins</s> (proponents of unity) among the <s>tīrthikas</s> (non-Buddhist teachers).

body.text: apare vadanti / sarvaṃ pṛthak / kuta iti cet / yathā śiraḥpadādi kāyātpṛthak / api ca lakṣaṇapṛthaktaṃ yathā vṛṣabho 'śvavilakṣaṇaḥ / tasmātsarvaṃ pṛthagiti jñeyam / iti pṛthagvādinastīrthikāḥ /
body.translated_text: Others say: everything is separate. Why? Just as the head, feet, and so on are separate from the body. Moreover, they are separate by their distinguishing characteristics, just as a bull is distinct from a horse. Therefore, everything should be known as separate — thus [speak] the <s>Pṛthagvādins</s> (proponents of separateness) among the <s>tīrthikas</s>.

body.text: atha kathaṃ sarvamekaṃ sadbhāvāditi / yataḥ saddhi dvedhā cetanamacetanañca / tatkathamekaṃ hetuvaiṣamyāṃditi / evaṃ dharmāṇāṃ samāsato dūṣaṇam /
body.translated_text: Now, how [can one say] that everything is one through its quality of existence? Because what exists is indeed twofold — conscious (<s>cetana</s>) and non-conscious (<s>acetana</s>). Then how can it be one, given the dissimilarity of causes? Thus is the refutation of [these] doctrines in brief.

body.text: yadi punaḥ kaścidvadedduḥkhasamudayanirodhamārgadvādaśanidānasaṃskṛtādidharmāṇāmekatvaṃ pṛthaktaṃ veti sarvametadasaddhetukam / kasmāt / yadyekatvaṃ tadā duḥkhāntavādāpattiḥ / yadi pṛthaktaṃ tadā sukhāntavādāpattiḥ / tasmāduktaṃ [ekatve pṛthakte vā]ntadvayavādāpattiḥ / naiṣa buddhadharmasyārtha iti /
body.translated_text: If someone were to say: whether the <s>dharmas</s> of suffering (<s>duḥkha</s>), origination (<s>samudaya</s>), cessation (<s>nirodha</s>), path (<s>mārga</s>), the twelve links of dependent origination (<s>dvādaśanidāna</s>), the conditioned (<s>saṃskṛta</s>), and so forth are one or separate — all of this is based on a false cause. Why? If they are one, then the fallacy of the doctrine of the end of suffering would follow. If they are separate, then the fallacy of the doctrine of the end of happiness would follow. Therefore it is said: whether in oneness or separateness, the fallacy of the doctrine of two extremes follows. This is not the meaning of the <s>Buddha</s>-<s>Dharma</s>.

body.text: api ca yathā kecidvadanti nirvāṇabhāvaḥ na duḥkhaṃ na ca sukham / kathaṃ jñātamiti cet / sarve hi dharmāścetanāḥ saduḥkhasukhā nirvāṇaṃ tvacetanaṃ kathaṃ sukhaṃ syāt /
body.translated_text: Moreover, as some say: the state of <s>nirvāṇa</s> is neither suffering nor happiness. How is this known? Because all <s>dharmas</s> that are conscious have suffering and happiness, but <s>nirvāṇa</s> is non-conscious — how could it be happiness?

body.text: api ca kecidvādinaḥ sukhaṃ vadanti / kuta iti cet / sukhaṃ trividham / sukhavedanāsukhaṃ, anupaghātaḥ, anākāṅkṣā ca / nirvāṇa ākāṅkṣābhāvānnirvāṇaṃ sukham /
body.translated_text: Moreover, some proponents say it is happiness. Why? Happiness is threefold: the happiness of pleasant sensation (<s>sukhavedanā</s>), the absence of harm (<s>anupaghāta</s>), and the absence of craving (<s>anākāṅkṣā</s>). Since in <s>nirvāṇa</s> there is no craving, <s>nirvāṇa</s> is happiness.

body.text:
(#Uh 9#)
api ca nirvāṇaṃ nityamiti mayā pūrvaṃ jñātam / idānīntu [vaktavyaṃ] saṃskārebhyastat pṛthak na veti kecit / atrocyate / nirvāṇaṃ nityamiti pūrvaṃ jñātaṃ kimucyate saṃksāraistattulyam / saṃskārāṇāṃ svabhāvaḥ pariṇāmaḥ pradhvaṃsaśca / nirvāṇabhāvasya tu nityatā sukhatvañca / kathaṃ vidvāṃstatsaṃskāraistulyaṃ vadet /
body.translated_text: (Uh 9) Moreover, '<s>nirvāṇa</s> is permanent' — this I have previously understood. Now, [the question to be addressed is] whether it is separate from the <s>saṃskāras</s> (conditioned formations) or not — so say some. To this it is replied: that <s>nirvāṇa</s> is permanent was previously understood — why is it said to be the same as the <s>saṃskāras</s>? The nature of <s>saṃskāras</s> is transformation and destruction. But the state of <s>nirvāṇa</s> has permanence and the quality of happiness. How would a wise person say that it is the same as the <s>saṃskāras</s>?

body.text: anyacca kecidāhuḥ / ātmabhāvasya rūpavattve nityo 'nityo vāyamiti na niścīyate /
body.translated_text: And others say: as to whether the self (<s>ātman</s>) has form (<s>rūpa</s>) [or not], whether it is permanent or impermanent — this cannot be determined.

body.text: atrocyate / sarvaṃ mūrtamanityameva yathā murto ghaṭo vināśī / ātmāpi tadvaditi cettadānitya eva / ātmano mūrtatvantu sūtrairna samarthitaṃ, yuktihīnañcaitat / yathā ratnabudhyā sikatopalādānaṃ tathā bhavato vacanamatīva mithyā / atha kasmādātmāmurta iti cenmayā pūrvamuktaṃ ghaṭo mūrtatvādvināśīti / yadyātmaivaṃ syāt, tadā so 'pi vināśī bhavet / kathamidānīṃ bhavatā pṛcchyate `kasmādātmāmūrta' iti /
body.translated_text: To this it is replied: everything material (<s>mūrta</s>) is indeed impermanent, just as a material pot is perishable. If the self is likewise [material], then it too is indeed impermanent. But the materiality of the self is not established by the <s>sūtras</s>, and this lacks reasoning. Just as picking up pebbles thinking them to be gems, so your statement is extremely false. But why [do you say] the self is immaterial? I have previously stated that a pot is perishable because of its materiality. If the self were likewise, then it too would be perishable. How then do you ask 'Why is the self immaterial?'

body.text: aparañca / aniyatasiddhāntalakṣaṇam, yathā kaścit pṛcchet / kiṃ śabdo vastu[bhūto] nityo 'nityo vā / atrocyate / yadvibhāganiṣpannaṃ tadanityameva / śabdo 'pi vibhāganiṣpannaḥ kathaṃ nityo bhavet /
body.translated_text: And another [topic]: the characteristic of an indeterminate thesis — for example, if someone asks: is sound, as a real entity, permanent or impermanent? To this it is replied: whatever is produced through differentiation is indeed impermanent. Sound also is produced through differentiation — how could it be permanent?

body.text: atha kiṃ nāma śabdo vastu[bhūtaḥ] / atrocyate / aniścaye kathaṃ praśnaḥ /
body.translated_text: Now, what indeed is sound as a real entity? To this it is replied: in [a state of] uncertainty, how can there be a question?

body.text: atha kiṃ kevala evātmānāgate 'dhvani sukhaduḥkhe vedayate saśarīro vā /
body.translated_text: Now then, does the self alone experience happiness and suffering in the future, or does it do so with the body?

body.text: atrocyate / etasmiccharīre vinaṣṭa ātmano 'parasmiñcharīre vedanam /
body.translated_text: To this it is replied: when this body is destroyed, the self experiences [happiness and suffering] in another body.

body.text:
(#Uh 10#)
nanu ka eṣa ātmā yo 'nāgate 'dhvani sukhaduḥkhe vedayate / atrocyate / 'ātmā, iti pūrvamuktaṃ bhavatā / kathaṃ punaḥ sannasan vātmā' iti pṛcchyate / ayuktametat /
body.translated_text: (Uh 10) But who is this self that experiences happiness and suffering in the future? To this it is replied: 'The self' — this was previously stated by you. How then is it asked 'whether the self exists or does not exist'? This is improper.

body.text: atha siddhāntārtha uktaḥ / kiṃ punarvākyapraśaṃsālakṣaṇam / atrocyate / yuktyaviruddhamanadhikamanyūnamadhigatapadārthaṃ vacanadharmanibaddhaṃ prasiddhadṛṣṭāntāviruddhamananuyojyañca / ebhirhetubhirvākyapraśaṃsetyucyate /
body.translated_text: Now the meaning of the established doctrine has been stated. What then is the characteristic of the commendation of a proposition? To this it is replied: it is not contradicted by reasoning, is neither excessive nor deficient, the meanings of words are well-understood, it is bound by the rules of expression, it is not contradicted by well-known examples, and it is not subject to objection. By these reasons, a proposition is said to be commendable.

body.text: nanu kiṃ nāma yuktyaviruddham / atrocyate / vijñānamevātmeti kecinmanyante sarvaskārāṇāṃ śūnyatvādanātmatvācca / na hi sarve saṃskārā vijñānamiti tadayuktam / saṃskārā hi vijñānasya hetavaḥ / hetūnāṃ cānātmatvāt, kathaṃ vijñānamātmā /
body.translated_text: But what is meant by 'not contradicted by reasoning'? To this it is replied: some think that consciousness (<s>vijñāna</s>) alone is the self, since all <s>saṃskāras</s> (conditioned formations) are empty and without self. But not all <s>saṃskāras</s> are consciousness — therefore this is improper. For <s>saṃskāras</s> are the causes of consciousness. Since the causes are without self, how can consciousness be the self?

body.text: atha sarve dharmāṃ anityāḥ śabdastu naiva sarvaṃ, tasmācchabdo nitya iti / atrocyate / bhavatā sarvamityuktam, ko 'rthaḥ punaḥ śabdasya, yo naiva sarvam / etadahetukamayuktañca /
body.translated_text: Now, [if someone says] all <s>dharmas</s> are impermanent, but sound is not everything, therefore sound is permanent — to this it is replied: you have said 'everything,' but what is the meaning of 'sound, which is not everything'? This is without reason and improper.

body.text: anyacca / sarve kṛtakadharmā anityā eva / agnisantānavat / śabdo 'pi tathā / tasmādanityaḥ / etadaviruddhalakṣaṇam /
body.translated_text: And further: all <s>dharmas</s> that are produced (<s>kṛtaka</s>) are indeed impermanent, like the continuity of fire. Sound is likewise. Therefore it is impermanent. This is the characteristic of [an argument that is] not contradicted.

body.text: atha kimanadhikamanyūnañca / atrocyate / ahikanyūnatvayorlakṣaṇaṃ pūrvamuktam / nyūnatvaṃ trividham hetunyūnatvaṃ vākyanyūnatvaṃ dṛṣṭāntanyūnatvañca / yadi kaścidvadet / ṣaḍvijñānanyanityāni ghaṭavat / kāraṇantu na vadettadā taddhetunyūnatvamityucyate / yadi kaścidvadeheho 'yamanātmā sakāraṇatvāt / śabdo 'pyanātmā sakāraṇatvādetadṛṣṭāntanyūnatvam /
body.translated_text: Now, what is 'neither excessive nor deficient'? To this it is replied: the characteristics of excess and deficiency have been stated previously. Deficiency is threefold: deficiency of reason (<s>hetu</s>), deficiency of proposition (<s>vākya</s>), and deficiency of example (<s>dṛṣṭānta</s>). If someone were to say: the six consciousnesses (<s>vijñānas</s>) are impermanent, like a pot — but does not state the reason, then that is called 'deficiency of reason.' If someone were to say: this body (<s>deha</s>) is without self (<s>anātman</s>), because it has a cause; sound too is without self, because it has a cause — this is 'deficiency of example.'

body.text:
(#Uh 11#)
yadi kaścidvadedanityāni catvāri mahābhūtāni ghaṭavatkṛtakāni / etadvākyanyūnatvam / etadvīparītaṃ tu sampannamityucyate /
body.translated_text: (Uh 11) If someone were to say: the four great elements (<s>mahābhūtas</s>) are impermanent, like a pot, because they are produced — this is 'deficiency of proposition.' The opposite of this is called 'complete' (<s>sampanna</s>).

body.text: sampannañca yathā / ātmavādyevaṃ praṣṭavyaḥ / yaduktaṃ bhavatātmeti sa nityo 'nityo vā / yadyanityastadā saṃskāravadvināśadharmā / nitya iti cettarhi kathaṃ nirvāṇaspṛhā / etat sampannalakṣaṇam /
body.translated_text: And what is 'complete' is as follows: the proponent of the self (<s>ātmavādin</s>) should be questioned thus — you have stated 'the self' (<s>ātman</s>); is it permanent or impermanent? If impermanent, then like the <s>saṃskāras</s>, it has the quality of being perishable. If permanent, then how [can there be] a desire for <s>nirvāṇa</s>? This is the characteristic of 'completeness.'

body.text: atha kiṃ nāmādhikam / atrocyate / adhikaṃ trividham, hetvadhikaṃ, dṛṣṭāntādhikaṃ, vākyādhikañca / yadi kaścidvadecchabdo 'nityaḥ samyogajaḥ / yathā ghaṭaḥ kṛtako 'nityaśca / punarapi vadecchabda ākāśasya guṇaḥ / ākāśo 'mūrtaḥ śabdastu rūpadharmā kathamanyonyasamāśrayaḥ / etaddhetvadhikam yadyucyate pañcendriyāṇyanityāni pratidhvanivatkṛtakatvāt / śabdo 'pi tathā / kathaṃ tajjñāyate / oṣṭhamukhādisamudbhavatvāt / tadṛṣṭāntādhikam / yadyucyate 'ṇuḥ sūkṣma ākāśastu vyāpī / ubhāvapi nityau / śabdastu na tathā tasmādanitya etadṛṣṭāntādhikam / api ca śabdo 'nityaḥ sakāraṇatvāt / nitya iti cet, tadayuktam / kasmāt? dvābhyāṃ hetubhyām / murtodbhavatvādaindriyakatvācca / kathaṃ nitya iti yacca samānadharmakaṃ tatsarvamanityam / etadvākyādhikamucyate /
body.translated_text: Now, what is 'excess'? To this it is replied: excess is threefold — excess of reason (<s>hetu</s>), excess of example (<s>dṛṣṭānta</s>), and excess of proposition (<s>vākya</s>). If someone were to say: sound is impermanent because it is produced from conjunction; just as a pot is produced and impermanent; and then further says: sound is a quality of space (<s>ākāśa</s>); space is formless, but sound has the quality of form — how can they be mutually dependent? This is 'excess of reason.' If it is said: the five sense faculties are impermanent, like an echo, because they are produced; sound is likewise — how is this known? Because it arises from the lips, mouth, and so forth. This is 'excess of example.' If it is said: the atom (<s>aṇu</s>) is subtle, but space is all-pervading; both are permanent; but sound is not like that, therefore it is impermanent — this is 'excess of example.' Moreover, sound is impermanent because it has a cause. If [someone says] it is permanent, that is improper. Why? For two reasons: because it arises from material [sources], and because it is sensory. How can it be permanent? And whatever has the same qualities is entirely impermanent. This is called 'excess of proposition.'

body.text: atrāha / kīdṛśaṃ vākyaṃ laukikānāṃ pratipādanāya smartham / ucyate / yadi mūrkhāya gambhīrārtha vadedyathā sarve dharmā śūnyāḥ śāntā nirātmāno niṣpugdalā māyāvat nirmāṇavattattvarahitā ityādi tadā taṃ gambhīrārthaṃ vidvāneva jñātuṃ śankoti pṛthagjanastu śrutvā bhrāntyāpanno bhavet / (#Uh 12#) etadaprāptakālam / athocyate / asti dharmāṇāṃ karma, asti viṣākro 'sti ca bandhamokṣaḍiḥ / yaḥ karoti so 'nubhuṅkta ityalpabuddhayo 'pi śrutvāvagacchanti yathā vedhakāraṇisaṃyogenāgnerūtpattiḥ / yadabhidhīyate tadyadi sattvopayogi bhavet, tadā sarveṣāṃ [tatra] pratītiranumodanañca / etat prāptakālam /
body.translated_text: Here one asks: what kind of statement is capable of instructing ordinary people? It is replied: if one were to speak profound meaning to a fool — such as 'all <s>dharmas</s> are empty, peaceful, without self, without <s>pudgala</s> (person), like an illusion, like a magical creation, devoid of essence,' and so forth — then only a learned person would be able to understand that profound meaning, but an ordinary person (<s>pṛthagjana</s>), upon hearing it, would become confused. (Uh 12) This is 'untimely' (<s>aprāptakāla</s>). But [if] it is said: there is <s>karma</s> (action) of <s>dharmas</s>, there is the fruit of action (<s>vipāka</s>), and there is the way of bondage and liberation; whoever acts, that one experiences [the result] — even those of little understanding can comprehend this upon hearing, just as fire arises from the conjunction of a piercing instrument and wood. Whatever is stated, if it is beneficial to beings, then there is the acceptance and approval of all. This is 'timely' (<s>prāptakāla</s>).

body.text: atha kiṃ pratipattiḥ / ucyate / abhihitasya bāhulye 'pi smaraṇasāmarthyam, arthānāṃ gāmbhīrye 'pi tallakṣaṇopalabdhiḥ, janaprītikaraśca sādhyasāraḥ / yathā kaścidvadet sarve dharmāḥ śūnyā anīśvarāḥ sarvavastūnāṃ pratītyasamutpannatvāditi pratipattiḥ /
body.translated_text: Now, what is comprehension (<s>pratipatti</s>)? It is replied: the ability to remember even when what has been stated is extensive; the apprehension of the defining characteristics even when the meanings are profound; and the essence of what is to be established should be pleasing to people. For example, if someone were to say: all <s>dharmas</s> are empty and without a lord (<s>anīśvara</s>), because all things are dependently originated (<s>pratītyasamutpanna</s>) — this is comprehension.

body.text: atha ke vākyadoṣāḥ / atrocyate / pūrvoktaviparītā vākyadoṣāḥ / vākyadoṣāḥ punardvividhāḥ / kiñca taddvaividhyam / arthasyābhede punaruktiḥ / vākyasya cābhede punaruktiriti / kā nāmaikārthapunaruktiḥ / yathā kauśika ityuktvā punarvadeddevendraḥ śakraḥ purandaro veti / iyamucyata etasyaivārthasya nāmāntarapunaruktiḥ /
body.translated_text: Now, what are the faults of statements (<s>vākyadoṣa</s>)? It is said here: the faults of statements are the opposites of the previously stated [virtues]. Furthermore, faults of statements are of two kinds. What is this twofold classification? Repetition when the meaning is the same, and repetition when the sentence is the same. What is repetition of a single meaning? For example, having said '<s>Kauśika</s>' (descendant of Kuśika), one says again '<s>Devendra</s>,' '<s>Śakra</s>,' '<s>Purandara</s>' — this is called repetition through synonyms of the same meaning.

body.text: nāmārthatulyatā yathā / indra ityuktvā punarapīndra iti vadet / iyaṃ nāmārthābhede punaruktiḥ /
body.translated_text: Equivalence of name and meaning is as follows: having said '<s>Indra</s>,' one says '<s>Indra</s>' again. This is repetition when both name and meaning are identical.

body.text: yadalaṅkṛtamasaṅgaṃ voktaṃ sa sarvo vākyadoṣa ityucyate / aparañca yadyuktisamupetamapyakramam eṣo 'pi vākyadoṣa iti /
body.translated_text: Whatever is spoken without ornament and without coherence — all of that is called a fault of statement. Moreover, whatever is accompanied by reasoning but lacks proper sequence — that too is a fault of statement.

body.text: yathā gāthayoktam /
body.translated_text: As stated in the verse:

body.text: yathā kaściddevānāmindrasya śakrasya bhāryāṃ praśaṃmayan suvarṇarūpiṇīm //
body.translated_text: For example, someone praising the wife of <s>Indra</s>, king of the gods, [says she is] golden-complexioned,

body.text:
(#Uh 13#)
komalapādahastāṃ paścācca śakro devānāmindro 'suratripuravināśīti tu vadannityakramaṃ vacanamuktam /
body.translated_text: with delicate feet and hands — and then afterwards says '<s>Śakra</s>, king of the gods, is the destroyer of the <s>Asura</s> [city] <s>Tripura</s>' — such a statement violates the proper sequence.

body.text: atha katividhaṃ pramāṇam / caturvidhaṃ pramāṇam / pratyakṣamanumānamupamānamāgamaśceti / caturṣu pramāṇeṣu pratyakṣa śreṣṭham / kutaḥ punaḥ pratyakṣaṃ śreṣṭhamiti cedapareṣāṃ trayāṇāṃ pramāṇānāṃ pratyakṣopajīvakatvācchreṣṭham / yathā dṛṣṭe dhūmavatyagnau paścāddhumadarśanādagneranumānam / tasmātpratyakṣaṃ viśiṣyate / yatha ca marīcidarśanenodakopamānam / tasmātpratyakṣe pūrvaṃ jñāte paścādupamānalābhaḥ / .....paścātpratyakṣakāle pūrvajñānaṃ satyam /
body.translated_text: Now, how many kinds of <s>pramāṇa</s> (means of valid knowledge) are there? There are four kinds of <s>pramāṇa</s>: <s>pratyakṣa</s> (direct perception), <s>anumāna</s> (inference), <s>upamāna</s> (analogy), and <s>āgama</s> (scripture/testimony). Among the four <s>pramāṇas</s>, <s>pratyakṣa</s> is the foremost. Why is <s>pratyakṣa</s> the foremost? Because the other three <s>pramāṇas</s> depend upon <s>pratyakṣa</s>, it is foremost. For example, having directly seen fire accompanied by smoke, afterwards, upon seeing smoke [alone], one infers fire. Therefore, <s>pratyakṣa</s> is superior. And as when seeing a mirage, one makes an analogy to water — therefore, <s>upamāna</s> (analogy) is obtained only after <s>pratyakṣa</s> is first known. .....afterwards, at the time of direct perception, the prior knowledge [is confirmed as] true.

body.text: tataśca pratyakṣādeva [pramāṇa]trayaṃ jñānamiti jñātam / idānīntu tatpratyakṣaṃ kathaṃ saditi / atrocyate / pañcendriyajñānaṃ kadācinmithyā / yattu sādhyavasāyaṃ samyagdharmāvabodhakaṃ tatparamam / grīṣme marīcīnāmalātacakragandharvanagarāṇāṃ ca pratyakṣe 'pi tadasat /
body.translated_text: Thus it is known that the three [other] means of knowledge arise from <s>pratyakṣa</s> (direct perception) itself. But now, how is this <s>pratyakṣa</s> valid? It is said here: the knowledge of the five senses is sometimes false. But that which involves firm determination and correctly reveals the nature of <s>dharmas</s> — that is supreme. In summer, even though mirages, fire-wheels [optical illusions], and <s>gandharva</s>-cities (mirages) are directly perceived, they are unreal.

body.text: aparañca / lakṣaṇāspaṣṭatvāddarśanabhramaḥ / yathā rātrau sthāṇuṃ dṛṣṭvā manuṣya eṣa ityucyate / aṅgulyā cakṣuḥpīḍanācca dvicandradarśanam / śūnyatājñāne prāpte samyagdṛṣṭirucyate / jñāta pratyakṣaṃ tāvat / atha kimanumānalakṣaṇam / ucyate tatpūrvamuddiṣṭam / adhunā vyākhyāyate / anumānaṃ trividhaṃ pūrvavat, śeṣavat, sāmānyato [dṛṣṭaṃ] ca / yathā ṣaḍaṅguliṃ sapiḍakamūrdhānaṃ bālaṃ dṛṣṭvā paṣcāddhṛddhaṃ bahuśrutaṃ devadattaṃ dṛṣṭvā ṣaḍaṅgulismaraṇāt so 'yamiti pūrvavat /
body.translated_text: Furthermore: due to the indistinctness of the marks, there is error in perception. For example, seeing a post at night, one says 'This is a person.' And by pressing the eye with a finger, one sees two moons. When knowledge of <s>śūnyatā</s> (emptiness) is attained, it is called right view (<s>samyagdṛṣṭi</s>). Thus <s>pratyakṣa</s> (direct perception) has been explained. Now, what is the definition of <s>anumāna</s> (inference)? It is said: it was indicated earlier; now it will be explained in detail. <s>Anumāna</s> is of three kinds: <s>pūrvavat</s> (from prior [cause to effect]), <s>śeṣavat</s> (from remainder), and <s>sāmānyato dṛṣṭa</s> (from general observation). For example, having seen a child with six fingers and a pimple on his head, and later seeing <s>Devadatta</s> as an elder and learned man, by recollecting the six fingers, one infers 'This is the same person' — this is <s>pūrvavat</s>.

body.text: śeṣavat yathā, sāgarasalilaṃ pītvā tallavaṇarasamanubhūya (#Uh 14#) śeṣamapi salilaṃ tulyameva lavaṇamiti / etaccheṣavadanumānam /
body.translated_text: <s>Śeṣavat</s> is as follows: having drunk ocean water and experienced its salty taste, one infers that the remaining water too is equally salty. This is <s>śeṣavat</s> (inference from remainder).

body.text: sāmānyato dṛṣṭaṃ yathā / kaścigdacchaṃstaṃ deśaṃ prāpnoti / gagane 'pi sūryācandramasau pūrvasyāṃ diśyuditau paścimāyāñcāstaṃ gatau / tacceṣṭāyāmadṛṣṭāyāmapi tadgamanamanumīyate / etatsāmānyato dṛṣṭam / nanu kā śrutiḥ / atrocyate, satyaprācīnavṛddhabuddhabodhisattvadarśanādāryasūtradharmaśravaṇagrahaṇayorjñānadarśanotpādasāmarthyameṣā śrutirityucyate / yathā suvaidyako bheṣajakuśalo maitracittena śikṣakaḥ suśruta ityucyate /
body.translated_text: <s>Sāmānyato dṛṣṭa</s> (inference from general observation) is as follows: someone who walks reaches that place. In the sky too, the sun and moon, having risen in the east, set in the west. Even though the actual movement is not seen, their motion is inferred [from the change of position]. This is <s>sāmānyato dṛṣṭa</s>. Now, what is <s>śruti</s> (authoritative testimony)? It is said here: through the vision of true, ancient, venerable, awakened ones and <s>bodhisattvas</s>, the capacity that produces the arising of knowledge and vision from hearing and grasping the noble <s>sūtras</s> and <s>Dharma</s> — this is called <s>śruti</s>. Just as a skilled physician, expert in medicine, who teaches with a benevolent mind, is called <s>Suśruta</s> ('well-heard'),

body.text: evamapi yat kṛtasarvadharmasākṣātkārairmahājñānairāryaiḥ śrutaṃ tat suśrutamucyate /
body.translated_text: in the same way, what is heard (<s>śruta</s>) by the noble ones of great knowledge who have realized all <s>dharmas</s> directly — that is called <s>suśruta</s> (well-heard/authoritative).

body.text: atha kimupamānalakṣaṇam / atrocyate / yathā sarve dharmā śūnyāḥ śāntā māyāvat nirmāṇavat / saṃjñādāntāśvavat, saṃskārāḥ kadalīvat, kāmalakṣaṇaṃ piḍakavat viṣavat / etadupamānamucyate / evaṃ catvāro hetavaḥ / tadavagamanaṃ hetujñānamityuktam /
body.translated_text: Now, what is the definition of <s>upamāna</s> (analogy)? It is said here: for example, all <s>dharmas</s> are empty (<s>śūnya</s>), peaceful, like a magical illusion (<s>māyā</s>), like a magical creation (<s>nirmāṇa</s>); perceptions (<s>saṃjñā</s>) are like a tamed horse; <s>saṃskāras</s> (formations) are like a plantain tree; the mark of desire (<s>kāma</s>) is like a boil, like poison. This is called <s>upamāna</s>. Thus there are four means of proof (<s>hetu</s>). Understanding these is called knowledge of reasons (<s>hetujñāna</s>).

body.text: atha ke hetvābhāsāḥ / atrācyate / hetvābhāsā eteṣu vādadharmesu mahādoṣā eva jñeyāḥ / śīghrañcāpahartavyāḥ / athedānīṃ hetvābhāsā vyākhyāsyante / hetvābhāsānāṃ lakṣaṇānyaparimitāni saṃkṣepatastvaṣṭāveva / vākchalaṃ, sāmānyachalaṃ, saṃśayasamaḥ, kālātītaḥ, prakaraṇasamaḥ, varṇyasamaḥ, savyabhicāraḥ, viruddhaḥ /
body.translated_text: Now, what are <s>hetvābhāsas</s> (fallacious reasons)? It is said here: <s>hetvābhāsas</s> in these rules of debate should be understood as great faults. They should be quickly refuted. Now the <s>hetvābhāsas</s> will be explained. The characteristics of <s>hetvābhāsas</s> are unlimited, but in brief there are eight: <s>vākchala</s> (verbal quibble), <s>sāmānyachala</s> (quibble based on generality), <s>saṃśayasama</s> (equal to doubt), <s>kālātīta</s> (untimely), <s>prakaraṇasama</s> (equal to the topic under debate), <s>varṇyasama</s> (equal to what is to be proved), <s>savyabhicāra</s> (deviating), and <s>viruddha</s> (contradictory).

body.text: nanvete 'ṣṭau dharmā vistareṇa vivektavyāḥ / ucyate / nava iti caturvidham / navaḥ, nava, na vaḥ, nava iti /
body.translated_text: Now, these eight categories should be explained in detail. It is said: '<s>nava</s>' has four [possible] meanings: '<s>navaḥ</s>' (new), '<s>nava</s>' (nine), '<s>na vaḥ</s>' (not yours), and '<s>nava</s>' [as a mere sound].

body.text:
(#Uh 15#)
yathā kaścidāha / yo maya parihitaḥ sa navakambalaḥ / atra dūṣaṇaṃ (vadet) yadbhavatā parihitaṃ tadekameva vastraṃ kathaṃ naveti / atra prativedenmayā nava ityuktaṃ tathāca navaḥ kambalaḥ natu naveti / atra dūṣayetkathaṃ nava? navalomairnirmitatvānnava ityukte prativādī vadet tattvato 'parimitāni lomāni kathaṃ navalomānītyucyate /
body.translated_text: For example, someone says: 'The blanket worn by me is a <s>nava</s>-blanket (new blanket).' Here the objection [could be]: 'What you are wearing is only a single garment — how can it be nine (<s>nava</s>)?' Here one would respond: 'I said <s>nava</s> meaning new (<s>navaḥ</s>), not nine (<s>nava</s>).' Here the objector would say: 'How is it new (<s>nava</s>)? Since it is made of new wool, it is called <s>nava</s>.' The opponent would reply: 'In reality, the hairs [of wool] are innumerable — how can they be called nine (<s>nava</s>) hairs?'

body.text: atrāha / nava iti mayā pūrvamuktaṃ na tu navasaṃkhyā / atra dūṣaṇam / tadvastraṃ yuṣmākameveti jñātaṃ kasmādetanna vaḥ kathyate / atrottaram / mayā nava ityuktaṃ kintu na va iti noktam / atra dūṣaṇam / bhavataḥ kāyaṃ kambalo vasta iti pratyakṣametat / kathamucyate na vaḥkambalaḥ / ayaṃ hetvābhāsa ityucyate vākchalaṃ ca /
body.translated_text: Here one says: 'I said <s>nava</s> meaning new, not the number nine.' Here the objection: 'That garment is known to be yours — why is it not called "yours" (<s>vaḥ</s>)?' Here the reply: 'I said <s>nava</s>, but I did not say <s>na vaḥ</s> (not yours).' Here the objection: 'The blanket covers your body — this is directly perceived. How can you say it is "not yours" (<s>na vaḥ</s>)?' This is called a <s>hetvābhāsa</s> (fallacious reason), and it is also <s>vākchala</s> (verbal quibble).

body.text: aparañca vākchalam / yathā girirdahyata ityukte, dūṣaṇam / tattvatastṛṇataravo dahyante kathaṃ girirdahyata ityuktam / etadvākchalamityucyate /
body.translated_text: Here is another example of <s>vākchala</s> (verbal quibble): when someone says 'The mountain is burning,' the objection is: 'In reality, it is the grass and trees that are burning — how can it be said that the mountain is burning?' This is called <s>vākchala</s>.

body.text: api ca chalaṃ dvividhaṃ / pūrvavat sāmānyañceti / yathā / saṃskṛtā dharmāḥ śrūnyāḥ śāntā ākāśavadityukte, dūṣaṇam / yadyevaṃ, ubhayorapi śūnyatvamabhāvaśca, tadā niḥsvabhāvā dharmā ākāśatulyā iti sāmānyachalam /
body.translated_text: Moreover, <s>chala</s> (quibble) is of two kinds: <s>pūrvavat</s> (as before) and <s>sāmānya</s> (based on generality). For example, when it is said 'Conditioned <s>dharmas</s> are empty (<s>śūnya</s>), peaceful, like space (<s>ākāśa</s>),' the objection is: 'If so, since both are empty and non-existent, then <s>dharmas</s> without intrinsic nature are equal to space.' This is <s>sāmānyachala</s> (quibble based on generality).

body.text: kā tāvadutpattiriti / atrocyate / sata utpattiriti / yathā mṛdo ghaṭatvattvāddhaṭotpādakatvam / yadi mṛdo ghaṭatvavattvaṃ tadā mṛdeva ghaṭaḥ syāt / tadā tadutpattaye kṛtaṃ kumbhakārarajjucakrasaṃyogena / yadi mṛdaḥ sadbhāvena ghaṭotpādakatvaṃ, tadodakasyāpi sadbhāvena ghaṭotpādakatvaṃ (#Uh 16#) syāt / yadyudakasya sadbhāvena ghaṭānutpādakatvaṃ kathaṃ tarhi mṛdo ghaṭotpādakatvam / iti sāmānyachalam /
body.translated_text: What then is origination? It is said here: there is origination from what exists. For example, because clay has the nature of a pot, it has the capacity to produce a pot. But if clay has the nature of a pot, then clay itself would be the pot — and then what need would there be for the conjunction of the potter, the cord, and the wheel for its production? If clay produces a pot by virtue of its [mere] existence, then water too, by virtue of its existence, should be capable of producing a pot. If water, by virtue of its existence, does not produce a pot, then how does clay produce a pot? This is <s>sāmānyachala</s> (quibble based on generality).

body.text: kiṃ nāma saṃśayahetvābhāsalakṣaṇam / ucyate / sthāṇormanuṣyasādṛśyāt, rātrau taṃ dṛṣṭvā, eṣa sthāṇuḥ puruṣo veti vimarśaḥ / ayaṃ saṃśayahetvābhāsa iti /
body.translated_text: What is the definition of the <s>saṃśaya-hetvābhāsa</s> (fallacy of doubt)? It is said: due to the resemblance of a post to a person, upon seeing it at night, there arises the deliberation 'Is this a post or a person?' This is called <s>saṃśaya-hetvābhāsa</s> (the fallacy of doubt).

body.text: kaḥ punaḥ kālātītahetvābhāsaḥ / ucyate / yathā kaścidvadennityaḥ śabdaḥ / śabdamayatvādvedo 'pi nitya iti / atra dūṣaṇam / idānīṃ bhavatā śabdasya nityatākāraṇamapratiṣṭhāpya kathaṃ vedo nitya ityucyate /
body.translated_text: What then is the <s>kālātīta-hetvābhāsa</s> (fallacy of untimeliness)? It is said: for example, someone argues 'Sound is eternal, and since the <s>Vedas</s> are composed of sound, the <s>Vedas</s> too are eternal.' Here the objection is: 'You have now failed to establish the reason for the eternality of sound — how then can you say the <s>Vedas</s> are eternal?'

body.text: atra vadedyathākāśamarūpatvānnityaṃ tathā śabdo 'pyarūpatvānnityaḥ / tadvacane paścādapyukte so 'rthaḥ sidhyati / atra dūṣaṇaṃ kālatītametadvacanam / yathā gṛhe dagdha udākānveṣaṇaṃ bhavatopyevamiti kālātītaḥ /
body.translated_text: Here one would argue: 'Just as space is eternal because it is formless, so too sound, being formless, is eternal.' Even if this statement is made afterwards, that meaning is established. Here the objection is: this statement is untimely (<s>kālātīta</s>). Just as searching for water after the house has burned — so too is your [argument]. This is [the fallacy of] untimeliness.

body.text: atha ko nāma prakaraṇasamaḥ? (ātmanaḥ) śarīra bhinnatvādātmā nityaḥ / yathā (ghaṭasya) ākaśabhinnatvādvaṭo 'nityaḥ / ayaṃ prakaraṇasama ityucyate /
body.translated_text: Now, what is <s>prakaraṇasama</s> (the fallacy of being equal to the topic)? [One argues:] 'The <s>ātman</s> (self) is eternal because it is different from the body.' [Another argues:] 'Just as the pot is impermanent because it is different from space.' This is called <s>prakaraṇasama</s>.

body.text: atra dūṣaṇam / yadyātmā śarīrabhinnatrvānnitya iti, tadā (ghaṭasya) ākāśabhinnatvādvaṭo 'nityaḥ / ayam prakaraṇasama ityucyate / atra dūṣaṇam / yadyātmā śarīrabhinnatvānnitya iti, tadā (ghaṭasya) śarīrabhinnatvādvaṭo 'pi nityaḥ syāt śarīrabhinnatve 'pi ghaṭo 'nitya iti cet, tarhyātmāpi śarīrabhinnatvāt kathaṃ nityaḥ / iti prakaraṇasamaḥ /
body.translated_text: Here the objection: if the <s>ātman</s> is eternal because it is different from the body, then the pot is impermanent because it is different from space — this is called <s>prakaraṇasama</s>. Here the objection: if the <s>ātman</s> is eternal because it is different from the body, then the pot too, being different from the body, should be eternal. If [you say] the pot is impermanent despite being different from the body, then how is the <s>ātman</s> eternal [simply] because it is different from the body? This is <s>prakaraṇasama</s> (the fallacy of being equal to the topic).

body.text: ko nāma varṇyasamaḥ / ucyate / yathā nityamākāśamasparśatvāt / manovijñānamapi tathā / ayaṃ varṇyasama ityucyate /
body.translated_text: What is <s>varṇyasama</s> (the fallacy of being equal to what is to be proved)? It is said: for example, 'Space is eternal because it is intangible.' 'Mind-consciousness (<s>manovijñāna</s>) is likewise [intangible, hence eternal].' This is called <s>varṇyasama</s>.

body.text: kaḥ savyabhicāraḥ / ucyate / yathā pañcaviṣayā anityā (#Uh 17#) indriyagrāhyatvāt / catvāri mahābhūtānyapi tathā tasmādanityāni /
body.translated_text: What is <s>savyabhicāra</s> (the deviating fallacy)? It is said: for example, 'The five sense-objects are impermanent because they are graspable by the senses. The four great elements (<s>mahābhūtas</s>) are likewise [graspable], therefore they too are impermanent.'

body.text: atra dūṣaṇam / kūrmaroma lavaṇagandhaśca nirābhāsamātraṃ manovijñānopalabhyatvātkimanityamiti savyabhicāraḥ /
body.translated_text: Here is the refutation: turtle-hair and the smell of salt are mere non-appearances, apprehensible only by mental consciousness (<s>manovijñāna</s>) — what [does it mean to say] 'impermanent'? This is deviation (<s>savyabhicāra</s>).

body.text: atha ko nāma viruddhaḥ / ucyate / viruddho dvividhaḥ / dṛṣṭāntaviruddho yuktiviruddhaśca / yathātmā nityo 'mūrtatvāt, vṛṣabhavat / ayaṃ dṛṣṭāntaviruddhaḥ /
body.translated_text: Now, what is 'contradicted' (<s>viruddha</s>)? It is replied: contradiction is twofold — contradicted by example (<s>dṛṣṭāntaviruddha</s>) and contradicted by reasoning (<s>yuktiviruddha</s>). For example: 'the self is permanent because it is formless, like a bull' — this is 'contradicted by example.'

body.text: yuktiviruddho yathā, brāhmaṇasya kṣatrakarmānupālanaṃ mṛgayādiśikṣā ca, kṣatriyasya dhyānasamāpattiriti yuktiviruddhaḥ / evambhūtau dharmāvajñā abuddhaiva satyaṃ manyante /
body.translated_text: 'Contradicted by reasoning' is as follows: a <s>brāhmaṇa</s> maintaining the duties of a <s>kṣatriya</s> and training in hunting and the like, or a <s>kṣatriya</s> [practicing] meditative attainment (<s>dhyānasamāpatti</s>) — this is 'contradicted by reasoning.' Such [persons], ignorant of the two <s>dharmas</s>, truly regard them as <s>abuddha</s> (unenlightened).

body.text: nanu kimaviruddham / atrocyate / etadbhinnamaviruddhamityabhidhīyate /
body.translated_text: But what is 'non-contradicted' (<s>aviruddha</s>)? To this it is replied: that which is different from these is called 'non-contradicted.'

body.text:
iti hetvābhāsāḥ /
// iti prathamaṃ prakaraṇam //
body.translated_text: Thus [are explained] the fallacious reasons (<s>hetvābhāsas</s>). // End of the First Chapter //

body.text:
(#Uh 18#)
atha dvitīyaṃ prakaraṇam /
body.translated_text: (Uh 18) Now the Second Chapter.

body.text: pūrvamaṣṭavidhā vādadharmā uktāḥ / atha nigraha[sthāna]dharmān vakṣyāmaḥ /
body.translated_text: Previously, the eightfold rules of debate (<s>vādadharmas</s>) were stated. Now we shall explain the rules of the points of defeat (<s>nigrahasthānadharmas</s>).

body.text: nanu katame vādadharmāḥ / (atrocyate) yathā catvāri mahābhūtāni prajñaptireva / kasmāt / rūpādidharmatvādeva / aparaḥ punarāha / catvāri mahābhūtāni tattvataḥ santi / kathametajjñātam / kāṭhinyaṃ pṛthivīdharmo yāvaccalatvaṃ vāyudharmaḥ / tatsaditi jñeyam / etacca prativiruddham / tasmādvivādaḥ / yathā vā / pṛthivī śarīrakāraṇameva / aparāṇi mahābhūtānyapi tathā / atra dūṣaṇam / pṛthivyādi sarvavastusādhanasamarthaṃ sat, kathaṃ śarīramātraṃ sādhayediti nātra vivādaḥ / yadyevaṃ na syāttadā vāda ityucyate /
body.translated_text: But what are the rules of debate? (To this it is replied:) for example, 'the four great elements (<s>mahābhūtas</s>) are mere designations (<s>prajñapti</s>).' Why? Because they have the characteristics of form (<s>rūpa</s>) and so forth. Another then says: 'the four great elements truly exist.' How is this known? Hardness is the characteristic of earth, and so on up to movement being the characteristic of wind. That exists — so it should be known. And this is mutually contradictory. Therefore there is a dispute. Or, for example: 'earth is indeed the cause of the body.' The other great elements are likewise. Here is the refutation: if earth and the rest are capable of producing all things, how can they produce merely the body? Thus there is no dispute here. If it were not so, then it would be called 'debate.'

body.text: nanu kāni nigrahasthānāni / (atrocyate) yathā śabdo nityo 'mūrtatvādākāśavat /
body.translated_text: But what are the points of defeat (<s>nigrahasthānas</s>)? (To this it is replied:) for example, 'sound is permanent because it is formless, like space (<s>ākāśa</s>).'

body.text: atra dūṣaṇam / yadyapi śabdo 'mūrtaḥ / tathāpyaindriyakaḥ, saṃpratighaḥ, ghaṭavatkṛtakaḥ / api tvākāśe 'kṛtake kathaṃ tadṛṣṭāntalābhaḥ / etannigrahasthānamityucyate /
body.translated_text: Here is the refutation: even if sound is formless, it is nevertheless sensory (<s>aindriyaka</s>), involves contact (<s>saṃpratigha</s>), and is produced like a pot. But since space is unproduced, how can it serve as an example for that? This is called a 'point of defeat.'

body.text: atha ghaṭo mūrta ityanityaḥ śabdasya tvamūrtatvāt kathaṃ tadṛṣṭāntalābhaḥ /
body.translated_text: Now, a pot is impermanent because it is material; but since sound is immaterial, how can [a pot] serve as an example for it?

body.text: atra dūṣaṇam / śabdo ghaṭabhinno 'pyaindriyakaḥ śrāvaṇatvāt / tasmādanityaḥ /
body.translated_text: Here is the refutation: even though sound is different from a pot, it is sensory because it is audible. Therefore it is impermanent.

body.text: nanu kasyārthasyānigrahasthānatvāpattiḥ / saṃskārā vijñānañca (#Uh 19#) kṛtakatvādanityam / nirvāṇamakṛtakatvānnityam / etadvākyaṃ samyakpadarasam / etaducyate 'nigrahasthānam /
body.translated_text: But in what case does the fallacy of a non-point-of-defeat apply? '<s>Saṁskāras</s> (conditioned formations) and <s>vijñāna</s> (consciousness) (Uh 19) are impermanent because they are produced. <s>Nirvāṇa</s> is permanent because it is unproduced.' This statement has correct word-meaning. This is called a 'non-point-of-defeat.'

body.text: nanu kiṃ vacanaṃ dūṣayitavyam / cuayte / vākyavaiparītyaṃ, asaddhetusthāpanaṃ, udāharaṇavaiṣamyañcaitaddūṣayitavyam /
body.translated_text: But what statement should be refuted? It is replied: reversal of the proposition (<s>vākyavaiparītya</s>), establishing [something] through a false reason (<s>asadhetusthāpana</s>), and dissimilarity of the example (<s>udāharaṇavaiṣamya</s>) — these should be refuted.

body.text: yatha saṃjñā saṃyojanocchedikā, ityukte kaścit pṛcchet / kathaṃ saṃjñā samyojanocchedikā / jñānasya saṃjñāta utpādaṃ pūrvamanutkā saṃjñāmātrakathanādvākyavaiparītyamitīdaṃ dūṣaṇīyam /
body.translated_text: For example, when it is stated: 'perception (<s>saṁjñā</s>) cuts off the fetters (<s>saṁyojana</s>),' someone asks: how does perception cut off the fetters? Since there is no prior mention of the arising of knowledge (<s>jñāna</s>) from perception, and [since] only the mention of perception [is given] — this is 'reversal of the proposition' and should be refuted.

body.text: nanu kathaṃ punaretadvākyamucyate / asidvasthāpanānnigrahasthānāpattijñāpanārthamuktam /
body.translated_text: But how is this statement to be understood? It is said for the purpose of making known that a point of defeat follows from establishing [something on] an unproven basis.

body.text: aparañca / anuyojyānanuyogaḥ / prativaktavye 'prativaktavyata / trirabhihitasya parairavijñātam / trirabhihitasya svayamavijñānam / etāni nigrahasthānāni /
body.translated_text: And further: not questioning what should be questioned; not responding when a response is required; when something stated three times is not understood by the opponent; when something stated three times is not understood by oneself — these are points of defeat.

body.text: anyacca / pareṇa vivadamānastadvikalatāṃ nāvagacchati / anyastu vadati / eṣo 'rthaḥ mithyaiva, kiṃ bhavānnopalabhate tadā nigrahasthānam /
body.translated_text: And another: while disputing with an opponent, one does not recognize his deficiency. But another says: 'This very meaning is false — do you not perceive it?' Then it is a point of defeat.

body.text: anyacca / parasya samyagarthe doṣasamārope 'pi nigrahasthānam /
body.translated_text: And another: even in the imputation of a fault to the opponent's correct meaning, there is a point of defeat.

body.text: anyacca / vādinoktaṃ sarvairvijñātamapyasāveva (prativādī) nāvagacchati cettadapi nigrahasthānam / praśno 'pi tadvat / etāni nigrahasthānāni vādasya mahākaṇṭakāni gambhīraduḥkhāni jñeyāni, drutañca heyāni /
body.translated_text: And another: if what was stated by the debater is understood by all, yet he himself (the respondent) does not understand it, then that too is a point of defeat. The same applies to the question. These points of defeat are the great thorns of debate, causing deep distress — they should be known and quickly avoided.

body.text: nanu praśnāḥ katividhāḥ / ucyate / trividhāḥ / yathā vacanasamaḥ, arthasamaḥ, hetusamaśca / yadi vādinastaistribhiḥ (#Uh 20#) praśnottarāṇi na kurvanti tadvibhrāntam / yadyeteṣāṃ trayāṇāmuttarāṇāmanyatamaṃ nyūnaṃ syāttadasampannam /
body.translated_text: But how many types of questions are there? It is replied: three types — the question equal to the statement (<s>vacanasamaḥ</s>), the question equal to the meaning (<s>arthasamaḥ</s>), and the question equal to the reason (<s>hetusamaḥ</s>). If the debaters (Uh 20) do not give answers to these three types of questions, that is confusion. If among the answers to these three, any one is deficient, that is incomplete.

body.text: yadi vadedahamevamprakārān trīn praśnānnāvagacchāmi mama yathājñānamanyonyaṃ praṣṭavyaṃ, tadādoṣaḥ /
body.translated_text: If one says: 'I do not understand these three types of questions; I should ask according to my understanding' — then there is no fault.

body.text: vākyasamaḥ yathā / ātmā nāstītyukte tadvākyāśrayeṇa praśnaḥ / ayaṃ vākyasama ityucyate /
body.translated_text: An example of 'equal to the statement': when it is stated 'the self does not exist,' a question based on that very statement — this is called 'equal to the statement.'

body.text: arthasamaḥ tanmatopādānamevāyamarthasama ityucyate /
body.translated_text: An example of 'equal to the meaning': the adoption of that very position — this is called 'equal to the meaning.'

body.text: hetusamaḥ / paramanogaterutpādakasya hetorjñāmayaṃ hetusama ityucyate /
body.translated_text: An example of 'equal to the reason': knowing the reason that produces the opponent's mental intention — this is called 'equal to the reason.'

body.text: evaṃ sāmarthye satye nigrahasthānamityucyate /
body.translated_text: When such capacity exists, it is called a 'point of defeat.'

body.text: yadyatidrutaṃ vadecchrotāraśca nāvagaccheyustadapi nigrahasthānam /
body.translated_text: If one speaks too rapidly and the listeners do not understand, that too is a point of defeat.

body.text: athaitāvamātramaparāṇi vā santi / atrocyate / santyeva yathā nyūnaṃ, adhikam nirarthakaṃ, aprāptakālaṃ, punaruktaṃ pratijñāsannyāsa ityādīni nigrahasthānānītyucyante /
body.translated_text: Now, are there only this many, or are there others? To this it is replied: there are indeed others, such as deficiency (<s>nyūna</s>), excess (<s>adhika</s>), meaninglessness (<s>nirarthaka</s>), untimeliness (<s>aprāptakāla</s>), repetition (<s>punarukta</s>), and abandonment of the thesis (<s>pratijñāsannyāsa</s>) — these and others are called points of defeat.

body.text: yadyevamādi pūrvapakṣī vadet, tadā nigrahasthānāpattiḥ /
body.translated_text: If the proponent (<s>pūrvapakṣin</s>) says such things, then the fallacy of a point of defeat applies.

body.text: atha pratijñāvirodhaḥ / yathā vijñānaṃ nityam / kasmāt / vijñānasya hi dvaividhyam / vijñānotpāttirvijñākriyā ca /
body.translated_text: Now, contradiction of the thesis (<s>pratijñāvirodha</s>): for example, 'consciousness (<s>vijñāna</s>) is permanent.' Why? Because consciousness is twofold: the arising of consciousness and the activity of consciousness.

body.text: ghaṭasyāpi dvaividhyam, ghaṭotpattirghaṭakriyā ca / evaṃ vijñānamutpādyamānameva sakriyaṃ tasmānnityam / ghaṭasya tūtpattyanantaraṃ sakriyatvam, tasmādanityatvam /
body.translated_text: A pot also is twofold: the production of a pot and the activity of a pot. Thus, consciousness, even while being produced, has activity, therefore it is permanent. But the pot has activity only after its production, therefore it is impermanent.

body.text: atra dūṣaṇam / utpattāveva sakriyatvānnityamiti ceddīpasyāpyutpattāveva sakriyatvānnityatvaprasaṅgaḥ / atha dīpaścakṣuṣā dṛṣṭaḥ syāt, śabdaśca śravaṇena śrūyata iti kathaṃ dṛṣṭāntopapattiḥ / etatpratijñāsannyāsanigrahasthānam /
body.translated_text: Here is the refutation: if [it is argued that consciousness] is permanent because it has activity at the very moment of arising, then a lamp too, having activity at the very moment of arising, would absurdly be permanent. Now, if a lamp is seen by the eye and sound is heard by the ear, how can the example be applicable? This is the point of defeat [called] 'abandonment of the thesis.'

body.text:
(#Uh 21#)
aparañca / kecidvadantyātmā nitya iti / kathaṃ jñātam / anaindriyakatvāt / yathā ākāśo 'naindriyakatvānnityaḥ /
body.translated_text: (Uh 21) And further: some say the self (<s>ātman</s>) is permanent. How is this known? Because it is non-sensory (<s>anaindriyaka</s>). Just as space (<s>ākāśa</s>) is permanent because it is non-sensory.

body.text: atra dūṣaṇam / paramāṇavo 'nindriyakā api tvanityāḥ /
body.translated_text: Here is the refutation: atoms (<s>paramāṇus</s>) too are non-sensory, yet they are impermanent.

body.text: atrocyate / ātmākṛtakatvānnityaḥ paramāṇavastu kṛtakatvādanityāḥ /
body.translated_text: To this it is replied: the self is permanent because it is unproduced (<s>akṛtaka</s>). But atoms are impermanent because they are produced.

body.text:
atra dūṣaṇam / anupalabdheriti bhavatā pūrvamuktam / adhunā cākṛtakatvādibyucyate / ayaṃ pratijñāvirodhaḥ /
nanūcyate 'haṃ virodhīti cedbhavāṃstu mama vacanaṃ pratikūlayan katham virodhau na syāt /
body.translated_text: Here is the refutation: 'because of non-apprehension' — this was previously stated by you. But now it is stated 'because of being unproduced,' and so forth. This is a contradiction of the thesis. [The opponent says:] 'But I do not say I am contradictory!' However, you contradict your own previous statement — how would there not be contradiction?

body.text: kiñca kathametadyuktisaham / yadvi viruddhamityucyate mayā, sā bhavata eva vacanasya pūrvoktenārthan pratikūlatā / tasmādviruddhamityuktam /
body.translated_text: Moreover, how is this tenable with reasoning? What I call 'contradicted' is the inconsistency of your own statement with its previously stated meaning. Therefore it is called 'contradicted.'

body.text: anyacca / bhavatā pūrvamuktamaspaṣṭatvānme saṃśaya utpanna iti / nāhaṃ bhavadvirodhītyevaṃ saṃśayena virodhaḥ / etadapi nigrahasthānamiti /
body.translated_text: And further: because what you previously stated was unclear, a doubt has arisen in me. I am not contradicting you — but a contradiction arises through such doubt. This too is a point of defeat.

body.text: // iti dvitīyaṃ prakaraṇam //
body.translated_text: // End of the Second Chapter //

body.text:
(#Uh 22#)
atha tṛtīyaṃ prakaraṇam /
body.translated_text: (Uh 22) Now the Third Chapter.

body.text: vādī prāha / yadi kaścidvadedasti sattvo yāvatsanti prāṇā asti jīva ityādi / kathaṃ jñātam / aindriyakatvāt / yathā nirupadhiśeṣanirvāṇasyendriyairanupalabdherabhāvaḥ sattvānāntu na tathā / tasmātsantyeva iti jñātam /
body.translated_text: The debater says: if someone states 'there is a being (<s>sattva</s>), there are vital breaths (<s>prāṇas</s>), there is a soul (<s>jīva</s>),' and so forth — how is this known? Because it is sensory. Just as <s>nirvāṇa</s> without remainder (<s>nirupadhiśeṣanirvāṇa</s>) is known to be non-existent because it is not apprehended by the senses. But beings are not like that. Therefore it is known that they exist.

body.text: atmā nityaḥ / yathārhattvaphalaṃ kasmiṃścideva kāle vidyamānamapi pūrvaṃ paścāccāvidyamānatvādabhāva iti jñāyate / yathā ca dvītīyo mūrdhā tṛtīyo hastaśca / abhūtvā bhāvāt prāgabhāvaḥ / bhūtvā tu vināśātpradhvaṃsābhāva iti jñāyate / ātmā tu na tathā tasmānnityaḥ /
body.translated_text: The self is permanent. Just as the fruit of <s>arhatship</s> (<s>arhattvaphala</s>), though existing at a certain time, is known to be non-existent because it does not exist before or after. And just as a second head or a third hand [are non-existent]. From coming-into-being after not having been, there is prior non-existence (<s>prāgabhāva</s>). But from destruction after having been, there is destructive non-existence (<s>pradhvaṁsābhāva</s>) — so it is known. But the self is not like that. Therefore it is permanent.

body.text: atra dūṣaṇam / yathā mūla[kīla]odakānyadṛśyatvānna sadityuktam / arhattva[phalasyāpi] tathātvameva na tvabhāvaḥ / etattu na bhavatā sākṣātkriyate /
body.translated_text: Here is the refutation: just as underground water, because of its invisibility, is not said to be non-existent — the fruit of <s>arhatship</s> is likewise; it is not [actually] non-existent. But this is not directly perceived by you.

body.text: nanu maivam / udakasya pṛthivyāvaraṇādadṛśyatvam / arhattva[phalasya tu] kenāvaraṇenādṛśyatvam / tasmāttadasaditi jñāyate /
body.translated_text: But it should not be so! Water is invisible because of the covering of earth. But through what covering is the fruit of <s>arhatship</s> invisible? Therefore it is known to be non-existent.

body.text: atra dūṣaṇam / yadbhavatoktaṃ [yathā] dvitīyasya mūrdhnastṛtīyasya hastasya cādṛśyatvāda[bhāvaḥ] arhattva[phalasyāpya]bhāvaḥ iti spaṣṭam / tadayuktam / dvitīyasya mūrdhno nāstitve 'pi tarhi na prathamasya nāstitvam / arhattva[phalaṃ] tu nāstyeveti tasyaivātyantābhāvaḥ / kathaṃ dṛṣṭāntatopapattiḥ / yacca bhavatoktamanupalabdhernirvāṇābhāvaḥ siddha iti tadapyayuktam / kiṃ nāma (mahā)śāgarodakasya binduparimāṇasyāśakyajñānatvāttadasaditi (#Uh 23#) vaktuṃ śakyate / yadyapi binduparimāṇaṃ na jñāyate tathāpyastyeva sāgaraḥ / nirvāṇasyāpi tathātvam / anupalabdhāvapi tattattvataḥ sadeva / asaditi cedvaktavyam tasya kāraṇam / yadi na śakyate vaktaṃ tadā bhavata evārthahāniḥ / ayamucyate yathādharmavādaḥ /
body.translated_text: Here is the refutation. What you said — that just as the non-existence [follows] from the invisibility of the second head and the third hand, so too the non-existence of <s>arhatva</s> (arhatship) [follows] — this is clear. But this is improper. Even though the second head does not exist, the first does not therefore not exist. But <s>arhatva-phala</s> (the fruit of arhatship) indeed does not exist — that itself is its absolute non-existence. How does the example support [this]? And what you said — that from non-apprehension the non-existence of <s>nirvāṇa</s> is established — that too is improper. Can it be said that because the drop-measure of the great ocean's water cannot be known, therefore it does not exist? Even though the drop-measure is not known, the ocean certainly exists. <s>Nirvāṇa</s> is likewise — even when not apprehended, it truly exists. If [you say] it does not exist, the reason must be stated. If it cannot be stated, then the loss of your position follows. This is called a <s>yathādharmavāda</s> (statement contrary to proper reasoning).

body.text: anyacca yadyanupalabdhernirvāṇasyāsattvaṃ, tadā parasya saṃśayaḥ / yathā rātrau taruṃ dṛṣṭvā citte saṃśayaḥ / eṣa sthāṇurvā manuṣyo veti / na khalū taruḥ sthāṇoḥ puruṣasya vo[palabdhau] niyato hetuḥ / anupalabdhireva nirvāṇasyābhāve niyato heturiti cennātra saṃśayasambhavaḥ /
body.translated_text: Moreover, if the non-existence of <s>nirvāṇa</s> [follows] from non-apprehension, then [there is] doubt for the opponent. Just as, upon seeing a tree-trunk at night, doubt arises in the mind — 'Is this a post or a person?' Surely the tree-trunk is not a fixed cause for the apprehension of either a post or a person. If [you say] non-apprehension alone is the fixed cause of <s>nirvāṇa</s>'s non-existence, then there is no room for doubt.

body.text: anyacca karmavipākāvināśāt, sadeva nirvāṇam / kuta iti cet / yathā davena girestarudāhe 'gnistadvināśahetuḥ / kaḥ punastasya karmavipākasya vināśaheturyena tadvinaśyate / nirvāṇalābhe tadā prahāniḥ /
body.translated_text: Moreover, because <s>karmavipāka</s> (the maturation of karma) is not destroyed, <s>nirvāṇa</s> indeed exists. How so? Just as in a forest fire, when the trees on the mountain are burned, the fire is the cause of their destruction. But what then is the cause of destruction of that <s>karmavipāka</s> by which it is destroyed? Upon the attainment of <s>nirvāṇa</s>, that [karma] is abandoned.

body.text: atrocyate / asti tattvato vināśahetuḥ / āvaraṇāttvanupalabdhaḥ /
body.translated_text: To this it is replied: there truly exists a cause of destruction, but because of <s>āvaraṇa</s> (obstruction) it is not apprehended.

body.text: atra dūṣaṇam / nirvāṇamapi sadāvaraṇāttvanupalabdham /
body.translated_text: Here is the refutation: <s>nirvāṇa</s> too exists but is not apprehended due to <s>āvaraṇa</s> (obstruction).

body.text: kiñca yadi vipākasya vināśaheturvartata iti cennocyate / tadā bhavato 'rthahāniḥ / yadyabhāvādvināśaheturanuktastadāvaraṇābhāvo 'pi kathamuktaḥ / evaṃ kāraṇairkarmāṇāmavināśo jñāyate /
body.translated_text: Furthermore, if a cause of destruction of <s>vipāka</s> (karmic maturation) does exist — why is it not stated? Then the loss of your position follows. If the cause of destruction is not stated due to [its] non-existence, then how is the non-existence of <s>āvaraṇa</s> (obstruction) also stated? Thus, through [such] reasoning, the indestructibility of <s>karmas</s> is known.

body.text: eṣa yathādharmavāda ityucyate /
body.translated_text: This is called a <s>yathādharmavāda</s> (statement contrary to proper reasoning).

body.text: pūrvapakṣī vadati / yadi sāgarodakasadbhāvānnirvāṇasadbhāvaḥ siddhastadā kiṃ dvitīyasyāpi mūrdhnaḥ sadbhāvo na sidhyati / dvitīyasyāpi mūrdhnaḥ sadbhāvo na siddha iti cet (#Uh 24#) kathaṃ nirvāṇasya sadbhāvaḥ / tasmādbhavatoktaḥ sāgarodakadṛṣṭāntaḥ nirvāṇasadbhāvaṃ sādhayituṃ na samarthaḥ / kiṃ dvitīyasya mūrdhnaḥ sadbhāvaṃ sādhayet /
body.translated_text: The <s>pūrvapakṣin</s> (opponent) says: if the existence of <s>nirvāṇa</s> is established from the existence of ocean water, then why is the existence of the second head not also established? If the existence of the second head is not established, then how is the existence of <s>nirvāṇa</s> [established]? Therefore, the ocean-water example cited by you is not capable of establishing the existence of <s>nirvāṇa</s> — rather it would [equally] establish the existence of the second head.

body.text: atra dūṣaṇam / kiṃ nirvāṇamasaditi bhavadabhipretam / asataḥ sattā vāsato 'sattā vā / asato 'satteti cet kathaṃ nirvāṇamasaditi pratijñāyate / yadi tvasataḥ sattā kathaṃ bhavatāsattocyate /
body.translated_text: Here is the refutation: is it your position that <s>nirvāṇa</s> is non-existent? [If so,] is it the existence of the non-existent or the non-existence of the existent? If [you say] the non-existence of the non-existent, then how is it asserted that <s>nirvāṇa</s> is non-existent? But if [you say] the existence of the non-existent, how can non-existence be asserted by you?

body.text: yadyasato nirvāṇasya sattā tadā svato 'sato 'sattvamapi saditi cet, kathaṃ na nirvāṇasadbhāvalāba ityatra heturvaktavyaḥ / yadi vaktuṃ na śakyate, tadā niścitameva nirvāṇaṃ saditi jñeyam / etadapi yathādharmavāda ityucyate /
body.translated_text: If <s>nirvāṇa</s>, being non-existent, [gains] existence, and if [you say] that which is essentially non-existent is also existent — then why is the attainment of <s>nirvāṇa</s>'s existence not [accepted]? The reason must be stated here. If it cannot be stated, then it should be known with certainty that <s>nirvāṇa</s> exists. This too is called a <s>yathādharmavāda</s> (statement contrary to proper reasoning).

body.text: nanvātmā nityo 'nityo vā / atmā 'kṛtakatvānnityaḥ, ghaṭādiṣṭu kṛtakatvādanityaḥ /
body.translated_text: Now, is the <s>ātman</s> (self) permanent or impermanent? The <s>ātman</s> is permanent because it is uncreated (<s>akṛtaka</s>); but pots and such are impermanent because they are created (<s>kṛtaka</s>).

body.text: atra dūṣaṇam / akṛtakatvādātmā nitya iti cettadayuktam / kasmāt / puruṣāṇāṃ saṃśayajanakatvāt / yadyakṛtakatvānnitya evātmeti tadā nityo 'nitya veti saṃśayasyāsambhavaḥ / saṃśayajanakatvāddoṣaḥ /
body.translated_text: Here is the refutation: if the <s>ātman</s> is permanent because it is uncreated, that is improper. Why? Because it generates doubt among people. If the <s>ātman</s> is permanent simply because it is uncreated, then there should be no room for the doubt 'is it permanent or impermanent?' Because it generates doubt, [there is] a fault.

body.text: vādī / iyaṃ doṣāpattirna mamaivāpi tu sarveṣāmeva vādināṃ yathā śabdo nityo 'mūrtatvāt / atītaḥ kāyo 'styeva pūrvanivāsānusmaraṇādityādipratijñā pūrvavatsaṃśayamutpādayatīti / tasmatsarvatraiva doṣāpattiḥ /
body.translated_text: The proponent says: this fault does not belong to me alone but to all debaters. Just as [the proposition] 'sound is permanent because it is formless,' or 'the past body certainly exists because of the recollection of former lives (<s>pūrvanivāsa-anusmaraṇa</s>),' and so forth — [each] proposition generates doubt just as before. Therefore, the fault applies everywhere.

body.text: atra dūṣaṇam / dṛṣṭānta eva saṃśayaṃ nirdhārayati / bhavatāṃ tūdāhṛto dṛṣṭānto mama saṃśayamutpādayati tasmādasiyo 'yaṃ dṛṣṭāntaḥ / dṛṣṭānte 'siddhe 'rthahāniḥ / tadeva nigrahasthānam /
body.translated_text: Here is the refutation: the example (<s>dṛṣṭānta</s>) itself resolves the doubt. But the example cited by you generates doubt in me — therefore this example is faulty. When the example is not established, the loss of the position [follows]. That itself is the <s>nigrahasthāna</s> (point of defeat).

body.text: yatpunarbhavatoktaṃ sarveṣāmeva doṣāpattirna tu mamaivetyeṣa (#Uh 25#) svadoṣa eva na tu paradoṣaḥ / kuta iti cet / yathā kaścidabhiyukta ātmānamaprakāśya sarva eva taskarā iti vadettadāsau puruṣa ātmānamapi taskaraṃ manyata iti jñeyam / bhavānapi tathā tasmānnigrāhyaḥ /
body.translated_text: As for your statement that the fault applies to all debaters and not to you alone — this is your own fault and not another's. How so? Just as if someone accused, without revealing himself, says 'everyone is indeed a thief' — then that person should be known as considering himself also a thief. You are likewise — therefore you are to be defeated.

body.text: idānīṃ yadi bhavānātmānaṃ prakāśayitumiḥcchu pūrvayuktimatikramya punarvaktumicchennūnaṃ bahudoṣāpattiḥ syāt / bhavataḥ prathamaḥ pakṣo dvitīyena [pakṣeṇa] dūṣitaḥ / tṛtīyaścārtho mayā dūṣitaḥ / pañcamena doṣāvadhimicchan pūrvaṃ nātikrāmedataḥ bhavato 'ntyaḥ pakṣaḥ punaruktaṃ bhavet / punaruktaṃ ca nigrahasthānam /
body.translated_text: Now, if you wish to reveal yourself and, having transgressed the previous reasoning, wish to speak again — then surely many faults would follow.
