Your first position has been refuted by the second [position]. And the third point has been refuted by me. Wishing to end the faults with the fifth [position], one should not transgress the earlier [ones] — therefore your final position would be mere repetition (<s>punarukta</s>). And repetition is a <s>nigrahasthāna</s> (point of defeat).

body.text: nanvanuyojyaḥ ṣaṣṭho 'pi?
body.translated_text: But should not the sixth also be examined?

body.text: atrocyate / sidvastāvatpañcamasya doṣaḥ / tatkathaṃ ṣaṣṭho 'nuyojyaḥ / asmin hi pratyukte pūrvadoṣatulyatā / anuyoktuḥ sadoṣatve pratipakṣeṇa tūṣṇīmbhaviṃtavyam /
body.translated_text: To this it is replied: the fault of the fifth has already been established. Then how can the sixth be examined? For in this reply, there is equality with the previous fault. When the examiner is faulty, the opponent should remain silent.

body.text: aparañca / ṣaṣṭhasya doṣaḥ pañcamenāparyanuyojyaḥ / kuta iti cet / pañcamenaiva hyeṣa ṣaṣṭho 'nuyuktaḥ / ato 'yaṃ svayame sadoṣaḥ kathaṃ taṃ dūṣayet / evaṃ saddharmavādaḥ /
body.translated_text: Furthermore, the fault of the sixth cannot be further examined by the fifth. How so? Because this sixth has already been examined by the fifth itself. Therefore, being itself faulty, how can it refute that [other]? Thus [is established] the <s>saddharmavāda</s> (true doctrine of debate).

body.text: // iti tṛtīyaṃ prakaraṇam //
body.translated_text: // Thus ends the third chapter. //

body.text:
(#Uh 26#)
athe caturthaṃ prakaraṇam /
body.translated_text: Now the fourth chapter.

body.text: nanu bhavatā vyākhyāto yathādharmasadvādaḥ / kaḥ punaḥ sambandhaḥ /
body.translated_text: Now, you have explained the true and false doctrines (<s>yathādharma</s> and <s>sadvāda</s>). But what is the connection [between them]?

body.text: atrocyate / praśnottarasambandho viṃśatividhaḥ / yadi kaścittena viṃśatividhenārthena samyagnyāyamārabhate sa sadvādasya jñātetyucyate / yadi naivaṃ tadā nāyaṃ vivādadharmāvagantā / eṣāṃ viṃśatividhānāṃ sāro dvividhaḥ / vaidharmyaṃ sādharmyañca / sajātīyatvātsādharmyaṃ vijātīyatvādvaidharmyam / arthasya hi tatsamāśrayatvātte viṃśatidharmān vyāpnuvataḥ /
body.translated_text: To this it is replied: the connection of question and answer (<s>praśnottara-sambandha</s>) is twenty-fold. If someone properly undertakes reasoning by means of these twenty types, he is said to be a knower of true doctrine (<s>sadvāda</s>). If not, then he is not one who understands the <s>dharma</s> of debate (<s>vivāda</s>). The essence of these twenty types is twofold: <s>vaidharmya</s> (dissimilarity) and <s>sādharmya</s> (similarity). Because of belonging to the same class, [there is] <s>sādharmya</s>; because of belonging to different classes, [there is] <s>vaidharmya</s>. Because the matter depends on both, those twenty <s>dharmas</s> are pervaded [by these two].

body.text: kiṃ sādharmyam / yathā kleśakṣayo nirābhāsa eva, ākāśabhāvo 'pi nirābhāsa iti sādharmyam /
body.translated_text: What is <s>sādharmya</s> (similarity)? For example, the destruction of <s>kleśas</s> (afflictions) is indeed without appearance (<s>nirābhāsa</s>); the nature of <s>ākāśa</s> (space) is also without appearance — this is <s>sādharmya</s>.

body.text: kiṃ vaidharmyam / yathā nirvāṇamakṛtakatvānnityaṃ tathā sarve saṃskārāḥ kṛtakatvādanityāḥ / iti vaidharmyam /
body.translated_text: What is <s>vaidharmya</s> (dissimilarity)? For example, <s>nirvāṇa</s> is permanent because it is uncreated (<s>akṛtaka</s>); but all <s>saṃskāras</s> (conditioned formations) are impermanent because they are created (<s>kṛtaka</s>) — this is <s>vaidharmya</s>.

body.text: nanu sādharmyavaidharmyābhyāṃ kathaṃ dūṣaṇam /
body.translated_text: But how is refutation (<s>dūṣaṇa</s>) [accomplished] by means of <s>sādharmya</s> and <s>vaidharmya</s>?

body.text: atrocyate / sādharmyadūṣaṇamicchatā evaṃ vaktavyam / rūpaṃ cakṣuṣā dṛṣṭaṃ, śabdastu śravaṇena śruta iti, kathaṃ tayoḥ sādharmyam / yadi rūpādbhinnaḥ śabdastadā rūpasyānityatvācchabdo nityo bhavet /
body.translated_text: To this it is replied: one who wishes to refute by <s>sādharmya</s> (similarity) should say thus — form (<s>rūpa</s>) is seen by the eye, but sound (<s>śabda</s>) is heard by the ear; how can there be similarity between them? If sound is different from form, then since form is impermanent, sound should be permanent.

body.text: vaidharmyadūṣaṇam / yatha rūpasyaindriyakatvādanityatā, ātmano 'naindriyakatvānnityatā /
body.translated_text: Refutation by <s>vaidharmya</s> (dissimilarity): just as form is impermanent because it is sensory (<s>aindriyaka</s>), the <s>ātman</s> (self) is permanent because it is non-sensory (<s>anaindriyaka</s>).

body.text: ghaṭasyātmanaśca sadbhāvaḥ / sadbhāvasādharmye ghaṭasyānityatvādātmano 'pi tathātvāpattiḥ / ghaṭasadbhāva ātmasadbhāvādbhinnastataścātmā (#Uh 27#) nityo ghātastvanitya iti cet / nityatāsādharmyada[pya]ātmanā nityena bhavitavyam /
body.translated_text: Both a pot and the <s>ātman</s> (self) have existence (<s>sadbhāva</s>). Through the similarity of existence, because the pot is impermanent, the <s>ātman</s> too would have the same [quality] — [one might counter:] the existence of the pot is different from the existence of the <s>ātman</s>, and therefore the <s>ātman</s> is permanent while the pot is impermanent. If so, then by the similarity of permanence too, the <s>ātman</s> should be permanent.

body.text: evaṃ dūṣaṇaṃ viṃśatividhaṃ yathā 1 utkarṣa[sama]m, 2 apakarṣa[sama]m, 3 bhedābheda[sama]m, 4 praśnabāhulyamuttarālpatā, 5 praśnālpatottarabāhulyam, 6 hetusamam, 7 kāryasamam, 8 vyāptisamam, 9 avyāptisamam, 10 kālasamam, 11 prāptisamam, 12 aprāptisamam, 13 viruddham, 14 aviruddham, 15 saṃśaya[sama]m, 16 asaṃśaya[sama]m, 17 pratidṛṣṭānta[sama]m, 18 śrutisamam, 19 śrutibhinnam, 20 anupapatti[sama]ñceti praśnottaradharmā viṃśatidhā /
body.translated_text: Thus refutation (<s>dūṣaṇa</s>) is twenty-fold, namely: 1. <s>utkarṣasama</s> (equalizing the superior), 2. <s>apakarṣasama</s> (equalizing the inferior), 3. <s>bhedābhedasama</s> (equalizing difference and non-difference), 4. excess of questions with deficiency of answers, 5. deficiency of questions with excess of answers, 6. <s>hetusama</s> (equalizing the reason), 7. <s>kāryasama</s> (equalizing the effect), 8. <s>vyāptisama</s> (equalizing pervasion), 9. <s>avyāptisama</s> (equalizing non-pervasion), 10. <s>kālasama</s> (equalizing time), 11. <s>prāptisama</s> (equalizing attainment), 12. <s>aprāptisama</s> (equalizing non-attainment), 13. <s>viruddha</s> (contradictory), 14. <s>aviruddha</s> (non-contradictory), 15. <s>saṃśayasama</s> (equalizing doubt), 16. <s>asaṃśayasama</s> (equalizing non-doubt), 17. <s>pratidṛṣṭāntasama</s> (counter-example), 18. <s>śrutisama</s> (equalizing scripture), 19. <s>śrutibhinna</s> (differing from scripture), 20. <s>anupapattisama</s> (equalizing impossibility) — these are the twenty types of question-and-answer <s>dharmas</s>.

body.text: 1. utkarṣa[sama]m / yathā (kaścidvaded), ātmā nitya indriyānupalabdheḥ / ākāśo hyanupalabdhernityaḥ / sarvamanupalabhyaṃ nityameva / ātmāpyanupalabhyaḥ kathaṃ tadanityatāprāptiḥ /
body.translated_text: 1. <s>Utkarṣasama</s> (equalizing the superior): for example, [if someone says:] the <s>ātman</s> (self) is permanent because it is not apprehended by the senses. For <s>ākāśa</s> (space), being not apprehended, is permanent. Everything that is not apprehended is indeed permanent. The <s>ātman</s> too is not apprehended — how then can impermanence apply to it?

body.text: atra dūṣaṇam / ākāśo 'cetanatvānnityaḥ / ātmā tu cetanaḥ kathaṃ nityaḥ / ākāśaścetana ityanyāyyam / yadyātmācetanastadaivākāśena sadharmā / evaṃ vidvāṃsaḥ so 'nitya iti manyante / etadutkarṣa[sama]m /
body.translated_text: Here is the refutation: <s>ākāśa</s> (space) is permanent because it is non-conscious (<s>acetana</s>). But the <s>ātman</s> (self) is conscious (<s>cetana</s>) — how can it be permanent? That space is conscious — this is unreasonable. If the <s>ātman</s> were non-conscious, then it would indeed share the same quality as space. Thus the wise consider it impermanent. This is <s>utkarṣasama</s> (equalizing the superior).

body.text: 2. apakarṣa[sama]m / yathākāśo 'cetana ātmā tu cetanaḥ / kathamākāśa ātmano dṛṣṭāntaḥ / etadapakarṣa[sama]m /
body.translated_text: 2. <s>Apakarṣasama</s> (the fallacy of disparagement): Just as space is non-conscious while the self is conscious — how can space be an example for the self? This is <s>apakarṣasama</s>.

body.text: 3. bhedābheda[sama]m / yathātmanityatāsthāpana ākāśa udāharaṇam / [atra dūṣaṇaṃ] ātmā ākāśaścābhinnau iti cedaikadharmyāt kathamākāśasyātmano dṛṣṭāntatā / (#Uh 28#) bhinnau iti cedanyānyasādharmyāprāptiḥ / etaducyate bhedābheda[sama]m /
body.translated_text: 3. <s>Bhedābhedasama</s> (the fallacy of difference and non-difference): As in establishing the eternality of the self, space is given as an example. [The objection is:] if the self and space are non-different, then because of their having a common property, how can space serve as an example for the self? (#Uh 28#) If [they are] different, then the attainment of similarity between mutually different things is not reached. This is called <s>bhedābhedasama</s>.

body.text: 4. anyacca / ātmā nityo 'naindriyakatvāt / yathākāśo 'nindriyakatvānnitya iti bhavataḥ sthāpanā /
body.translated_text: 4. And another: 'The self is eternal because it is beyond the senses, just as space is eternal because it is beyond the senses' — this is your thesis.

body.text: atha yadanaindriyakaṃ tannāvaśyaṃ nityam / tatkathaṃ siddham / etaducyate praśnabāhulyamuttarālpatā ca /
body.translated_text: But what is beyond the senses is not necessarily eternal. How then is it established? This is called excess of questions and deficiency of answers.

body.text: 5. anyacca / ātmā nityonaindriyakatvāditi bhavatsthāpanā / anaindriyakasya dvaividhyam / yathā paramāṇavo 'nupalabhyā anityāḥ / ākāśastvindriyānupalabhyo nityaśca / kathaṃ bhavatocyate yadanupalabhyatvānnitya ityucyate praśnālpatottarabāhulyañca /
body.translated_text: 5. And another: 'The self is eternal because it is beyond the senses' — this is your thesis. But what is beyond the senses is twofold: just as atoms are imperceptible yet impermanent, while space is imperceptible to the senses yet eternal. How can you say that because it is imperceptible it is eternal? This is called deficiency of questions and excess of answers.

body.text: 6. anyacca / anupalabdhihetunātmā nitya iti bhavatā pratijñātam / ākāśaścātmā ca bhinnauḥ kathamubhayoranupalabhyatvaṃ heturbhavet / iti hetusamam /
body.translated_text: 6. And another: you have proposed that the self is eternal by the reason of non-apprehension. But space and the self are different — how can non-apprehensibility serve as a reason for both? This is <s>hetusama</s> (the fallacy of equivalence of reason).

body.text: 7. anyacca / yatpañcamahābhūtamayaṃ tadanityam / ākāśa ātmā ca pañcamahābhūtamayau kathaṃ nityāvuktau / iti kāryasamam /
body.translated_text: 7. And another: whatever is composed of the five <s>mahābhūtas</s> (great elements) is impermanent. Space and the self are composed of the five <s>mahābhūtas</s> — how are they said to be eternal? This is <s>kāryasama</s> (the fallacy of equivalence of effect).

body.text: 8. anyacca / anupalabhyatvānnitya ākāśa iti bhavataḥ sthāpanā / ākāśaśca sarvavyāpī [tataśca] kiṃ sarvāṇi bastūnyanupalabhyāni / etadyāptisamam /
body.translated_text: 8. And another: 'Space is eternal because it is non-apprehensible' — this is your thesis. But space is all-pervading — [then] are all things non-apprehensible? This is <s>yāptisama</s> (the fallacy of over-pervasion).

body.text: 9. anyacca / paramāṇuravyāpyanaindriyako 'pyanityaḥ / ātmā tvanaindriyakaḥ kathaṃ nityaḥ / iti avyāptisamam /
body.translated_text: 9. And another: an atom is non-pervasive and beyond the senses, yet impermanent. The self, being beyond the senses — how is it eternal? This is <s>avyāptisama</s> (the fallacy of under-pervasion).

body.text: 10. anyacca / ātmā nityo 'nindriyakatvāditi bhavatsthāpanā / so 'yaṃ[hetu]rvartamāne 'tīte 'nāgate vā / atīta iti cedatītatvānnaṣṭāḥ / anāgata iti cedabhāvaḥ / vartamāna (#Uh 29#) iti cettadāhetuḥ / yathā śṛṅge yugapadeva jātatvānnānyonyahetuke / iti kālasamam /
body.translated_text: 10. And another: 'The self is eternal because it is beyond the senses' — this is your thesis. Is this reason [applicable] to the present, the past, or the future? If past, then by being past it is destroyed. If future, then it is non-existent. (#Uh 29#) If present, then at that time there is no cause — just as two horns, being born simultaneously, are not mutually caused. This is <s>kālasama</s> (the fallacy of temporal equivalence).

body.text: 11. anyacca / ātmā nityo 'naindriyakatvāditi bhavatsthāpanā / atha prāpyāprāpya vā heturiti / aprāpya cedasiddho hetuḥ / yathāgniraprāpya dahanāsamarthaḥ, asiścāprāpya chedanāsamarthaḥ / ātmānamaprāpya kathaṃ heturbhavet / ityaprāpti[samam] /
body.translated_text: 11. And another: 'The self is eternal because it is beyond the senses' — this is your thesis. Now, is the reason operative through contact or without contact? If without contact, the reason is unestablished — just as fire, without contact, is incapable of burning, and a sword, without contact, is incapable of cutting. Without reaching the self, how can it serve as a reason? This is <s>aprāptisama</s> (the fallacy of non-contact).

body.text: 12. anyacca / prāpya iti cet, prāpterahetutvam / iti prāptisamam /
body.translated_text: 12. And another: if [you say] through contact, then contact itself is not a reason [for eternality]. This is <s>prāptisama</s> (the fallacy of contact).

body.text: 13. anyacca / sarvamanityam / na tvātmā sarvaṃ, tato nitya iti bhavatpratijñā ātmā ca tadbhāvādanitya iti vaktavyaḥ, kiñciddagdho hi kambalaḥ prāyeṇādagdhatvādadagdha ityucyate / etadviruddham /
body.translated_text: 13. And another: everything is impermanent. But the self is not everything, therefore it is eternal — this is your thesis. But the self, being of that nature [i.e., belonging to 'everything'], should be called impermanent — just as a blanket that is partially burnt is called unburnt because it is mostly unburnt. This is <s>viruddha</s> (the contradictory fallacy).

body.text: 14. anyacca / ātmānaindriyakatvādākāśatulya iti bhavatsthāpanā / ākāśasyānupalabdhirātmano 'pi tathātvam / ātmana upalabdhiriti cettadākāśo 'pi sukhadūḥkhadikamupalabheta / ātmana ākāśasya cābhinnatvāt / etadaviruddham /
body.translated_text: 14. And another: 'The self is like space because it is beyond the senses' — this is your thesis. Space is non-apprehensible, and the self is likewise. If [you say] the self is apprehensible, then space too should apprehend happiness, suffering, and so forth, because of the non-difference of the self and space. This is <s>aviruddha</s> (the fallacy of [apparent] non-contradiction).

body.text: 15. anyacca / ātmanaḥ sadbhāvavannityatāniyatā / laukikānāṃ saṃśayasambhavo nityo 'nityo veti / etat saṃśayasamam /
body.translated_text: 15. And another: just as the existence of the self [is asserted], its eternality is undetermined. Among worldly people, doubt arises: is [the self] eternal or not? This is <s>saṃśayasama</s> (the fallacy of equivalence of doubt).

body.text: 16. anyacca / astyātmānaindriyakatvāditi bhavadvacanam atha vimarśaḥ kenāvaraṇenānupalabdhiḥ / kāraṇamatra vaktavyam / yadi kāraṇaṃ na vidyata ātmārthasya hāniḥ / ityasaṃśayasamam /
body.translated_text: 16. And another: 'The self exists because it is beyond the senses' — this is your statement. Now the inquiry: by what obstruction is there non-apprehension? The reason must be stated here. If no reason is found, then the thesis about the self is lost. This is <s>asaṃśayasama</s> (the fallacy of equivalence of non-doubt).

body.text:
(#Uh 30#)
17. anyacca / ātmānaindriyakatrvānnitya iti bhavatā pratijñātam / atha mūlakilodakānyanaindriyakānyapyanityānyātmā tu kathaṃ nityaḥ / iti pratidṛṣṭānta[sama]m /
body.translated_text: (#Uh 30#) 17. And another: 'The self is eternal because it is beyond the senses' — this you have proposed. But roots, stakes, and underground water are beyond the senses yet impermanent — how then is the self eternal? This is <s>pratidṛṣṭāntasama</s> (the fallacy of counter-example).

body.text: 18. anyacca / sūtreṣu ātmano 'nupalabdhiruktā tasmāttasya nityatā jñāteti bhavataḥ [sthāpanā] / (parantu) nāstyātmā nāstyātmīyamityapi sūtreṣūktam / nirgranthadharme cātmānityatoktā / ātmanityatve niyate sati sūtrāṇāṃ vaiṣamyānupapattiḥ / iti śrutisamam /
body.translated_text: 18. And another: 'In the <s>sūtras</s>, non-apprehension of the self is stated, therefore its eternality is known' — this is your thesis. But 'there is no self, there is nothing belonging to the self' is also stated in the <s>sūtras</s>. And in the <s>Nirgrantha</s> (Jain) doctrine, the self is said to be eternal. If the eternality of the self is fixed, then the contradiction among the <s>sūtras</s> is untenable. This is <s>śrutisama</s> (the fallacy of equivalence of scripture).

body.text: 19. anyacca / yadi bhavatā ekameva sūtramadhigacchatātmā nitya iti manyate / athānyeṣāmapi sūtrāṇāṃ pratīterātmānityo mantavyaḥ / ubhayathā pratītiriti cedekasyaivātmano nityatvānityatvaprasaṅgaḥ / iti śrutibhinnam /
body.translated_text: 19. And another: if you, having studied only one <s>sūtra</s>, think the self is eternal, then from the understanding of other <s>sūtras</s>, the self should be considered impermanent. If [you say] there is understanding both ways, then for the same self, both eternality and non-eternality would follow. This is <s>śrutibhinna</s> (the fallacy of divergent scripture).

body.text: 20. anyacca / yadi sadbhāvāditi hetunātmāstīti / atha śālasya sadbhāvāttāla utpadyate / yadyabhāvānnāstīti tadā tālabījeṣu vṛkṣākārābhāvāttadutpattyaprāptiḥ / sadbhāve 'nutpattiḥ / abhāve 'pyanutpattiḥ / ātmano 'pi tathātvam /
body.translated_text: 20. And another: if by the reason 'because of existence,' the self exists — then from the existence of a <s>śāla</s> tree, a palmyra should be produced. If because of non-existence it does not exist, then since the form of a tree is absent in palmyra seeds, its production cannot be attained. In existence, there is no production; in non-existence too, there is no production. The self is likewise.

body.text: yadi kiṃcitsadeva na tadānaindriyakatvaṃ hetutvena prayoktavyam / yadi ca sadeva tadā nānaindriyakatvena tasya sattā sādhyā / ityanutpattisamam /
body.translated_text: If something just exists, then imperceptibility should not be employed as a reason. And if it just exists, then its existence need not be proved through imperceptibility. This is <s>anutpattisama</s> (the fallacy of equivalence of non-origination).

body.text: yadi punaḥ kaścicchabdanityatāṃ sthāpayet, tadaivamvidhairuktapūrvairviśatiṃdharmaistadvadeva dūṣayet /
body.translated_text: If someone further were to establish the eternality of sound, one should refute it in the same way with these twenty previously stated properties.

body.text: nanvātmasadbhāvādeva bhavānātmānaṃ dūṣayati / ātmano 'bhāve kiṃ bhavatā dūṣaṇīyam / dūṣaṇāddhyasti dūṣayitavyam /
body.translated_text: Objection: you are refuting the self on the basis of the self's very existence. If the self does not exist, what is there for you to refute? For if there is refutation, there must be something to be refuted.

body.text: atra dūṣaṇam / yuktito nāsyātmā / bhavatā tu (#Uh 31#) tatsadbhāvasya vikalpānmayā bhavato dūṣaṇaṃ kṛtam / yadbhavatoktaṃ dūṣayitavyabhavādastyātmeti / tato dūṣaṇānnāstyātmeti jñātam / bhavata ātmaparigraha ātmābhāvadyotanarthamiti cettadayuktam / bhavadarthāprayogāt / idānīntu svayaṃ bhavatā mama siddhāntaḥ prayuktaḥ /
body.translated_text: Here is the refutation: by reasoning, there is no self. But because you conceive of its existence, I have made this refutation of your thesis. What you have said — 'the self exists because there is something to refute' — from that very refutation, it is known that the self does not exist. If [you say] your acceptance of the self is for the purpose of illuminating the non-existence of the self — that is improper, because your own thesis has not been applied. Now you yourself have employed my established doctrine.

body.text: nanu kathaṃ bhavatā jñātaṃ yanmayā bhavadarthaḥ parigṛhītaḥ / atra kāraṇaṃ vaktavyamiti cenmayā khalu pūrvamuktaṃ yatsvārthamaparigṛṇhatā bhavatā parasthāpanā parigṛhītā kathamidānīṃ punaridaṃ pṛcchyate / kathaṃ jñātaṃ yadbhavato 'rtho maya parigṛhīta iti / yato bhavadvacanaṃ viruddhaṃ tasmānnigrahasthānāpattiḥ /
body.translated_text: Objection: how have you known that I have adopted your thesis? If [you say] the reason must be stated here — I have indeed stated previously that by not accepting your own thesis, you have adopted your opponent's thesis. How is this question being asked again — 'How is it known that I have adopted your thesis?' Since your statement is contradictory, this leads to a <s>nigrahasthāna</s> (point of defeat).

body.text: anyacca / anaindriyakatvātsannevātmeti bhavatā pūrvaṃ pratijñātaṃ paścāttu dharmabāhulyena sādhitam / sthāpitahetoraniyatatvātpratijñāvirodhācca nigrahasthānam / tasmādbhavadarthanāhau yadi punarahaṃ kiṃcibdravīmi, [yanmayā] pūrvamuktaṃ tasmādetanna bhidyate / tadā vacanasya bahudoṣaprasaṅgaḥ / pakṣapratipakṣayoḥ pratipakṣamaryādā pañcame / tadatikramyoktaṃ vacanaṃ doṣaḥ / yadi vidvān gambhīraṃ nyāyaṃ bhāvayatyuktena dṛṣṭāntenārthāvagamasamarthaśca syāttadā tasya vāda evaṃvidhaṃ dharmaṃ nātikrāmati /
body.translated_text: And another: you first proposed 'The self exists because it is beyond the senses,' but later proved it through an excess of properties. Due to the inconclusiveness of the established reason and contradiction of the thesis, this is a <s>nigrahasthāna</s> (point of defeat). Therefore your thesis is negated. If I again say something, it does not differ from what I have previously said — then there would be the consequence of many faults of speech. In the relation of thesis and counter-thesis, the limit of the counter-thesis is five; a statement going beyond that is a fault. If a learned person contemplates profound logic and is capable of understanding the meaning through the stated examples, then his debate does not transgress this rule.

body.text: vādī prāha / evamukto vadadharmāṇāṃ sāraḥ / eṣa vādasāraḥ sarvavādānāṃ mūlam / etasmādvādātpakṣapratipakṣayoḥ paramotkarṣajñānaṃ jāyate / yathā bīje sukṣetra upte mūlāṅkurāḥ samṛddhāḥ / kukṣetre tūpte phalabhāva eva / etasya dharmasyāpi tathātvam /
body.translated_text: The debater said: thus stated is the essence of the rules of debate. This is the essence of debate, the root of all debates. From this debate arises the supreme knowledge of the excellence of thesis and counter-thesis. Just as when a seed is planted in a good field, roots and sprouts flourish, but when planted in a bad field, there is merely the appearance of fruiting — this rule too is likewise.

body.text:
(#Uh 32#)
yadi vidvān kaścit pramāṇavicārakuśalastadā vādānutpādayati / mūrkhastvalpabuddhiretadvādābhyāsenāpi tadavagamāsamarthastattvato vidvān nocyate / tasmādye ye sañjñānotpattiṃ subhāśubhavivekañcecchanti taistaireva saddharmavāda āśrayitavyaḥ /
body.translated_text: (#Uh 32#) If a learned person, skilled in the examination of <s>pramāṇas</s> (means of valid knowledge), produces debates [it is fruitful]. But a fool of little understanding, even through practice of this debate, is incapable of comprehending it — he is not called truly learned. Therefore, whoever desires the arising of true knowledge and the discrimination of good and bad must resort to debate on the true <s>Dharma</s>.

body.text: // iti caturthaṃ prakaraṇam //
body.translated_text: Thus ends the fourth chapter.

body.text: samāptaścāyaṃ granthaḥ /
body.translated_text: And this treatise is concluded.
